manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Centrifugation of Cell Culture LysateI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Centrifugation of Cell Culture Lysate to Separate Cell DebrisSubject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental BiologyObjective: To demonstrate how centrifugation separates insoluble cell debris from soluble components in a cell culture lysate, and to observe the formation of a pellet and clear supernatant.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrocentrifuge tube (1.5 mL), cloudy cell culture lysate, bench-top microcentrifuge, tube rack, gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves and lab coat. Place the microcentrifuge tube containing cloudy cell culture lysate into the tube rack and visually confirm the uniform cloudiness.2. Centrifugation: Place the tube into a balanced slot of the bench-top microcentrifuge. Close the lid and centrifuge at high speed (e.g., 10,000–14,000 × g) for a short time (about 1–2 minutes).3. Removal: After the centrifuge stops completely, carefully remove the tube without shaking it.4. Observation Position: Hold the tube upright at eye level for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before centrifugation, the lysate appears cloudy and uniformly mixed.2. After Centrifugation: A compact cell debris pellet forms at the bottom of the tube, while the liquid above becomes clear or translucent (supernatant).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCentrifugation separates cellular components based on size and density. Under high centrifugal force, heavier and insoluble materials such as cell debris sediment to the bottom of the tube to form a pellet, while lighter, soluble molecules remain in the supernatant. This principle is fundamental in cell and molecular biology for sample clarification prior to downstream analyses.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and Cooling2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe how the reading of a glass liquid thermometer changes when water is heated and then cooled, understand the relationship between temperature and thermal expansion of liquids, and recognize the response characteristics of a thermometer during heating and cooling processes.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass liquid thermometer (alcohol or mercury type), beaker A (heat-resistant, filled with room-temperature water), beaker B (filled with cool water), hot plate, thermometer clamp or stand, camera or mobile device for time-lapse photography, tripod, heat-resistant gloves (optional for safety).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place beaker A with water on the hot plate. Secure the glass liquid thermometer vertically using a clamp so that the bulb is fully immersed in the water but not touching the beaker bottom or walls. Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust the focus on the thermometer scale, and ensure the focus remains fixed for the entire time-lapse recording.2. Heating Stage: Turn on the hot plate to gently heat the water in beaker A. Start time-lapse recording. Observe the thermometer as the water temperature gradually rises.3. Transition Stage: After the thermometer reading has clearly increased and stabilized for a short time, carefully lift the thermometer out of beaker A (using gloves if needed).4. Cooling Stage: Immediately place the thermometer bulb into beaker B containing cool water. Continue time-lapse recording without changing camera position or focus.5. Completion: Observe until the thermometer reading clearly decreases and stabilizes. Turn off the hot plate and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The thermometer shows an initial temperature corresponding to room-temperature water; the liquid column is stable.2. During Heating: As the water in beaker A is heated, the liquid column inside the thermometer gradually rises, indicating an increase in temperature.3. During Cooling: After the thermometer is moved into beaker B with cool water, the liquid column gradually falls, indicating a decrease in temperature.4. Overall Observation: The rise and fall of the liquid column are continuous and directional, corresponding to heating and cooling.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the principle of thermal expansion of liquids. When the thermometer bulb is heated, the liquid inside expands more than the glass, causing the liquid column to rise along the scale, indicating a higher temperature. When placed in cool water, the liquid contracts as heat is transferred from the thermometer to the surrounding water, causing the liquid column to fall. The thermometer thus converts temperature changes into visible changes in liquid height.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the thermometer bulb does not touch the beaker walls or bottom to avoid measurement error or breakage.2. Heat the water gently to prevent sudden boiling or splashing.3. Keep the camera focus fixed throughout the experiment to ensure clear comparison in time-lapse images.4. Handle the hot beaker and thermometer carefully to avoid burns or damage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Temperature measurement using a liquid-in-glass thermometer based on thermal expansion. Minimum assumptions: heating increases temperature, cooling decreases temperature, and the thermometer liquid responds continuously and directionally. Phased storyline: (1) Initial stable thermometer reading in room-temperature water; (2) heating phase where water on a hot plate causes gradual rise of the liquid column; (3) transfer phase showing movement of the thermometer between beakers; (4) cooling phase where immersion in cool water causes gradual fall of the liquid column. Visibility constraints: thermometer scale and liquid column must remain clearly visible, camera focus fixed, and beaker context maintained to verify causal transitions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Soap Bubbles Tracing Rotating Air EddiesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Soap Bubbles Tracing Rotating Air Eddies in Gentle Indoor AirflowSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To visually demonstrate airflow patterns and rotating air eddies formed when gentle airflow passes a narrow vertical obstacle, using soap bubbles as tracers.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall desk fan (with adjustable low-speed setting), narrow vertical obstacle (e.g., thin cardboard strip or ruler fixed upright), bubble solution and bubble wand or bubble machine, tape or stand to fix obstacle, indoor room with still air.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the desk fan on a table and set it to the lowest steady speed. Fix the narrow vertical obstacle vertically about 10–20 cm in front of the fan outlet. Ensure the surrounding air is calm.2. Positioning: Stand or place the bubble source slightly upstream of the obstacle and offset to one side of the airflow.3. Core Operation: Turn on the fan to produce a gentle airflow. Release soap bubbles steadily into the airflow as it moves past the obstacle.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal DemonstrationSubject: Engineering - Computer ScienceObjective: To visually demonstrate level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a binary tree and understand how nodes are visited level by level from top to bottom and left to right.II. Experimental Materials and EnvironmentA simple binary tree diagram with 7 nodes labeled 1–7; light-colored background; animation or visualization tool capable of highlighting nodes and displaying an output list.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a simple complete binary tree with node 1 as the root, nodes 2 and 3 as its children, and nodes 4–7 as the third level, all on a light background.2. Initialization: Prepare an empty horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen.3. Core Operation: Begin level-order traversal.   a. Highlight the root node (1) in a bright color such as red; briefly apply a glow effect.   b. Append value 1 to the output list.   c. Move to the next level and highlight nodes 2 and 3 from left to right, one by one, each with a brief glow, appending their values in order.   d. Proceed to the third level and highlight nodes 4, 5, 6, and 7 from left to right, appending each value to the output list as it is visited.4. Completion: Stop the traversal when all nodes have been visited and the output list contains 1–7 in level-order.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All nodes are visible but unhighlighted; output list is empty.2. During Traversal: Nodes are highlighted level by level from top to bottom; within each level, nodes are highlighted from left to right; each highlight is followed by an update to the output list.3. Final State: All nodes have been highlighted once; the output list shows a complete left-to-right sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLevel-order traversal, also known as breadth-first traversal, visits nodes of a binary tree level by level starting from the root. It uses the principle of visiting all nodes at a given depth before moving to the next depth, typically implemented with a queue. The visualization demonstrates this principle by sequentially highlighting nodes by level and appending their values to an output list in the exact visiting order.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Binary tree level-order (breadth-first) traversal. Minimum assumptions: a static binary tree structure with fixed node positions and labels, and a visualization system capable of sequential highlighting and list updates. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 shows the full tree and empty output list; Phase 2 highlights the root and appends its value; Phase 3 highlights second-level nodes left to right with corresponding output updates; Phase 4 highlights third-level nodes left to right, completing the output list. Key causal transitions: node highlight represents a visit, which directly causes the node value to appear in the output list. Visibility constraints: the entire tree and the output list must remain visible throughout to verify order and correctness.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Salt Dissolves in Water but Not in OilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salt Dissolves in Water but Remains Undissolved in Oil2. Subject: Natural Science – Biology (Properties of Substances)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the solubility of table salt in water and in cooking oil through a simple side-by-side demonstration, and to understand that different liquids dissolve substances differently.II. Experimental Materials- Two identical clear glass containers (transparent, same size)- Clean water (left container)- Clear cooking oil (right container)- Table salt- Small spoon or fingers for sprinkling salt- Flat surface for placement- Camera or phone fixed on a tripod (for time-lapse or continuous recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical clear glass containers side by side on a flat surface. Pour the same amount of water into the left container and the same amount of clear cooking oil into the right container.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and angle so that both containers are clearly visible in the frame. Ensure lighting is sufficient and unchanged during recording.3. Adding Salt: Sprinkle an equal pinch of table salt into the water container and an equal pinch into the oil container at the same time.4. Swirling: Gently swirl both containers in the same manner for a few seconds to simulate mixing.5. Observation: Stop swirling and allow the containers to rest. Continue recording or observing for a short period.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In the water container: The salt grains gradually sink and then disappear, forming a clear solution with no visible solid salt remaining.2. In the oil container: The salt grains sink to the bottom and remain visible. They do not dissolve and may clump together.3. Comparison: After standing for a short time, the water remains clear with dissolved salt, while the oil remains clear but with undissolved salt at the bottom.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSalt is soluble in water because water molecules can surround and separate salt particles due to their polarity. Cooking oil is non-polar and cannot interact effectively with salt particles, so salt does not dissolve in oil and remains undissolved. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Saltwater vs Distilled Water Conductivity Comparison Using a Small MotorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Saltwater vs Distilled Water Conductivity Comparison Using a Small Motor2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Electrochemical Properties of Solutions)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the electrical conductivity of saltwater and distilled water by observing the operation of a small DC motor in a battery-powered circuit, and to understand how dissolved ions affect electrical conduction in aqueous solutions.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall DC motor (1), battery (1, 3–6 V), battery holder and connecting wires, two clear beakers (identical size), metal electrodes (2 pairs, e.g., graphite or stainless steel), saltwater solution (prepared by dissolving table salt in water), distilled water, switch (optional), insulating support, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Label the left beaker Saltwater and the right beaker Distilled Water. Pour equal volumes of saltwater and distilled water into the respective beakers.2. Circuit Setup: Connect the battery, switch (if used), and small DC motor in series with two branches leading to the electrodes. Ensure that each pair of electrodes will be immersed in one beaker, forming a complete circuit through the solution.3. Electrode Placement: Insert the metal electrodes into the saltwater beaker on the left, ensuring they do not touch each other. Insert the second pair of electrodes into the distilled water beaker on the right in the same manner.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position so that both beakers and the motor are clearly visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Core Operation: Close the switch or connect the battery to power the circuit, allowing current to pass through each solution and the motor.6. Observation and Recording: Observe the rotation speed and sound of the DC motor while the circuit is powered. Maintain the setup for several seconds to clearly capture differences.7. Completion: Disconnect the battery, remove the electrodes from the solutions, and turn off the camera. Dispose of solutions appropriately and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before powering the circuit, the motor is stationary; both solutions are clear and colorless.2. After Powering the Circuit: When current flows, the motor connected through the saltwater circuit rotates明显 faster or starts rotating clearly.3. Distilled Water Comparison: The motor connected through the distilled water circuit rotates very slowly or does not rotate at all.4. Overall Comparison: A clear contrast in motor performance is observed between saltwater and distilled water.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the dependence of electrical conductivity of aqueous solutions on the presence of ions. Saltwater contains dissolved sodium and chloride ions that act as charge carriers, allowing electric current to pass easily and drive the motor. Distilled water contains very few ions, resulting in extremely low conductivity and insufficient current to effectively power the motor. Therefore, the motor rotates strongly in saltwater but weakly or not at all in distilled water.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure electrodes in each beaker do not touch to avoid short circuits.2. Experiment Title: Detecting a Buried Metal Object with a Handheld Compass2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a buried metal object disturbs the local magnetic field and causes a measurable deflection of a handheld compass; to learn basic field methods for magnetic anomaly detection through systematic walking and sweeping observations.II. Observation During Second Pass: Observe whether compass deflections occur at approximately the same ground location as in the first pass.6. Completion: Mark or note the location where the strongest compass disturbance is observed. Compare observations from both directions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Ferromagnetic metal objects disturb the Earth’s local magnetic field.2. As the compass moves through this disturbed field, the needle responds by deflecting or rotating.3. Methodological Significance: By walking systematic straight lines and repeating measurements from opposite directions, random errors are reduced and the location of the magnetic anomaly can be confirmed.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the compass level to avoid mechanical error.2. Avoid carrying metal objects (keys, phones) near the compass.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparative Experiment of Impact Compaction and Static Compaction EffectsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Impact Compaction and Static Compaction EffectsSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To compare the compaction effects of static pressure and impact pressure on loose sand under the same load, and to understand the influence of loading mode on sand density and height.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical sand trays (A and B), loose dry sand, standard weight X, static loading plate, impact hammer or drop weight device (mass equal to X), ruler or scale, camera or mobile phone for demonstration photograph.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place sand trays A and B on a flat surface. Fill both trays with loose sand using the same method, and level the surface to ensure identical initial height and density.2. Static Compaction (Tray A): Place the loading plate on the sand surface of tray A. Slowly apply weight X vertically and keep it stationary for a fixed short time to produce static pressure.3. Impact Compaction (Tray B): Using the same weight X, apply impact loading by dropping or striking vertically onto the sand surface of tray B for several impacts.4. Measurement and Recording: After loading, remove the weights. Measure and record the final sand height in both trays, and visually compare surface settlement and compactness.5. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder the same load X, different loading methods produce different compaction effects. Static compaction applies stress slowly, allowing limited particle rearrangement. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Pointer vs LED Flashlight on a Rough WallI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Speckle and Interference from a Laser Pointer and an LED Flashlight2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the optical phenomena produced when coherent laser light and incoherent LED light illuminate a rough surface, and to understand speckle and interference as results of light coherence.II. Experimental EquipmentRed laser pointer (continuous beam), white LED flashlight, rough wall or matte surface (e.g., painted wall), camera or smartphone with manual focus, tripod or fixed support for camera, dark or dim room.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Darken the room to reduce ambient light. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the rough wall and set the camera focus manually so it remains fixed throughout the experiment.Setup: Hold the red laser pointer and the white LED flashlight side by side, aiming both beams at adjacent spots on the same rough wall.Core Operation: Turn on both light sources. Gently wiggle the laser pointer by hand while keeping the flashlight motion similar. Ensure the wall and camera remain completely stationary. Record a short time-lapse or continuous video.Completion: Stop the motion, turn off both light sources, and save the recorded images or video for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Laser Pointer: The illuminated spot appears as a granular, high-contrast speckle pattern. When the laser is wiggled, the speckle pattern shifts and changes rapidly, showing strong fluctuations.2. LED Flashlight: The illuminated area appears smooth and uniform, without a clear speckle pattern. Gentle wiggling causes only overall movement of brightness, not granular changes.3. Comparison: The difference between the dynamic speckle of the laser and the smooth illumination of the LED is clearly visible in the same frame.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLaser light is highly coherent, meaning the light waves maintain a fixed phase relationship. When laser light reflects from a rough surface, waves scattered from different points interfere with each other, producing a random speckle pattern. Wiggling the laser changes the interference conditions, causing the speckle to fluctuate. In contrast, LED light is incoherent and consists of many independent wave sources with random phases. As a result, interference averages out, and no stable speckle pattern is observed. This experiment demonstrates the role of coherence in optical interference and speckle formation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsDo not point the laser at eyes or reflective surfaces. Keep the camera and wall fixed to avoid confusing motion effects. Use gentle hand motion to clearly reveal speckle dynamics.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Optical coherence and its role in interference and speckle formation. Minimum assumptions: laser light is coherent, LED light is incoherent, and a rough wall causes scattering. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) initial illumination of wall by both sources; (2) appearance of granular speckle only in the laser spot; (3) gentle wiggling causes rapid speckle changes due to shifting interference paths; (4) LED spot remains smooth, showing only bulk motion. Visibility constraints: camera and wall must remain fixed, focus locked, and room dim so speckle contrast and differences are clearly observable.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Moving a Bar Magnet In and Out of a Coil Connected to a GalvanometerI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Electromagnetic Induction by Moving a Bar MagnetSubject: Physics – ElectromagnetismObjective: To observe induced current produced when a bar magnet moves relative to a coil, and to understand the basic law of electromagnetic induction through galvanometer deflection.II. Experimental EquipmentBar magnet (with marked N and S poles), copper wire coil, connecting wires, analog galvanometer (zero-centered), stand or hand-held setup.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Connect both ends of the copper wire coil firmly to the terminals of the analog galvanometer. Place the galvanometer so its needle is clearly visible and initially at zero.2. Initial Observation: Keep the bar magnet stationary outside the coil and observe that the galvanometer needle does not deflect.3. Core Operation A: Push the bar magnet straight into the center of the coil at a steady speed while observing the galvanometer needle.4. Core Operation B: Stop the magnet inside the coil and observe the needle returning to zero.5. Core Operation C: Pull the bar magnet out of the coil and observe the galvanometer needle again.6. Repeat: Change the speed or reverse the magnet’s pole and repeat the motion to compare needle deflections.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the magnet is stationary relative to the coil, the galvanometer needle stays at zero.2. When the magnet is pushed into the coil, the galvanometer needle deflects to one side.3. When the magnet is pulled out of the coil, the needle deflects to the opposite side.4. Faster motion of the magnet produces a larger needle deflection.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electromagnetic induction. When the bar magnet moves relative to the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing an electric current. The direction of the induced current depends on whether the magnetic flux is increasing or decreasing, which is reflected by opposite deflections of the galvanometer needle. This phenomenon follows Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law.VI. PrecautionsEnsure good electrical connections; move the magnet along the coil axis; avoid shaking the galvanometer; do not strike the meter needle.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Electromagnetic induction caused by changing magnetic flux through a conductor. Minimum assumptions: a visible bar magnet with distinct poles, a closed coil circuit, and a zero-centered analog galvanometer that responds instantly to induced current.Phased storyline for evaluation: (1) Initial static phase – magnet outside the coil, needle at zero. (2) Entry phase – magnet pushed into the coil, needle deflects in one direction. (3) Pause phase – magnet stationary, needle returns to zero. (4) Exit phase – magnet pulled out, needle deflects in the opposite direction. Key causal transition is that motion (not position) of the magnet causes needle deflection. Visibility constraints: the coil–galvanometer connection and needle movement must be clearly observable from a single stable viewpoint.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Verifying the Harmonic Mean Is Less Than the Arithmetic MeanI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparing Arithmetic Mean and Harmonic Mean2. Subject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To compute the arithmetic mean and harmonic mean of two positive numbers, plot both means on the same number line, and visually verify that the harmonic mean point is always below the arithmetic mean point.II. Experimental MaterialsPaper or whiteboard, pen or marker, ruler (optional), calculator (optional), graph paper or a simple number line.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Draw a small table with two columns labeled Number A and Number B. Choose two positive numbers, for example A = 2 and B = 8, and write them in the table.2. Arithmetic Mean Calculation: Write the formula AM = (A + B) / 2. Substitute the numbers step by step: (2 + 8) / 2 = 10 / 2 = 5. Record the result clearly.3. Harmonic Mean Calculation: Write the formula HM = 2 / (1/A + 1/B). Substitute step by step: 1/2 + 1/8 = 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8, then HM = 2 ÷ (5/8) = 16/5 = 3.2. Record the result clearly.4. Plotting: Draw a horizontal number line covering values from 0 to at least the larger number. Mark and label the arithmetic mean point at 5 and the harmonic mean point at 3.2 on the same line.5. Comparison: Observe the relative positions of the two points on the number line.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The arithmetic mean point appears to the right (higher value) on the number line.2. The harmonic mean point appears to the left (lower value) on the same number line.3. For the chosen positive numbers, the harmonic mean is clearly below the arithmetic mean.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFor any two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is always greater than or equal to the harmonic mean. The arithmetic mean averages values directly, while the harmonic mean gives more weight to smaller values through reciprocals. This mathematical property ensures that, when plotted on the same number line, the harmonic mean point is always lower than the arithmetic mean point.VI. Precautions1. Ensure both numbers are positive; harmonic mean is not defined for zero or negative values.2. Perform calculations step by step to avoid arithmetic errors.3. Clearly label points on the number line to avoid confusion.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: comparison of arithmetic mean and harmonic mean for two positive numbers, assuming basic arithmetic operations and number line representation. Expected phenomenon storyline: first, two positive numbers are presented in a table; second, the arithmetic mean is calculated step by step; third, the harmonic mean is calculated using reciprocals; fourth, both results are plotted on the same number line; finally, visual comparison shows the harmonic mean point below the arithmetic mean point. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Milk Protein Film Forming on a Heated Stainless Steel SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Milk Protein Film on a Heated Stainless Steel Plate2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer and Fouling Phenomena)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and visually observe the formation of a milk protein fouling film on a heated stainless steel surface under constant heating and flow conditions, and to understand the relationship between heat transfer, protein denaturation, and surface deposition using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentStainless steel plate (polished, food-grade), electric heating plate or heater (mounted below the steel plate), transparent circulation tray or flow cell, peristaltic pump or circulation pump, milk (standardized whole or skim milk), tubing, temperature controller and thermocouple, power supply, camera with tripod (fixed focus and fixed position), lighting source, protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Clean the stainless steel plate thoroughly with water and ethanol, dry it, and mount it horizontally above the heating plate. Place the transparent tray above the plate so that milk can flow evenly across the steel surface. Fix the camera position, angle, and focus; ensure the entire steel surface is in frame. Do not adjust focus during the experiment.2. System Setup: Connect the pump and tubing to form a closed-loop circulation system. Fill the system with milk, ensuring no air bubbles remain. Start milk circulation at a constant, low flow rate to create a thin, uniform film over the stainless steel surface.3. Heating Operation: Turn on the heater below the stainless steel plate and set a constant target temperature. Maintain stable heating throughout the experiment. Begin time-lapse recording once both flow and heating are stable.4. Continuous Operation: Allow milk to continuously circulate over the heated surface while heating is maintained. Do not disturb the setup. Observe the gradual change on the stainless steel surface through the transparent tray.5. Completion and Shutdown: After a clear fouling film is formed, stop heating first, then stop the pump. Save the time-lapse recording. Drain the milk, clean the system, and allow the equipment to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The stainless steel surface appears clean, smooth, and metallic; milk flowing across it is uniformly white and opaque, with no visible deposits.2. Early Heating Stage: After heating begins, no immediate visible change occurs, but slight dulling of the steel surface may appear in localized hot regions.3. Film Formation Stage: With continued heating, a thin, whitish or translucent film gradually forms on the stainless steel surface. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat-induced fouling caused by milk protein denaturation and deposition. Milk contains proteins such as whey proteins and casein. Denatured proteins lose their native structure, aggregate, and adhere to the metal surface, forming a fouling film. Gas Collection and Observation: Allow the generated gas to pass through the delivery tube into the fuchsine solution. Observe changes during heating.6. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Glass Etching with Hydrofluoric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Title: Glass Etching with Hydrofluoric Acid2. Subject: Chemistry – Chemical Reactions of Inorganic Materials3. Objective: To demonstrate selective etching of glass using hydrofluoric acid by masking with paraffin wax, observe surface changes, and understand the reaction principle.II. Equipment and ReagentsGlass slide; paraffin wax and applicator (wax pencil or melted wax); hydrofluoric acid solution (low concentration, demonstration use); plastic dropper; water for washing; tweezers; protective gloves, goggles; fume hood or simulated safe setup; camera or microscope with focusing and time-lapse capability.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear protective equipment. Clean and dry the glass slide.2. Masking: Draw a clear pattern on the slide surface using paraffin wax, ensuring covered areas are fully sealed.3. Etching: Place the slide flat. Using a dropper, carefully add hydrofluoric acid solution to cover the exposed (unwaxed) areas. Allow the slide to stand for a short, accelerated demonstration period.4. Washing: Pour off the acid into a designated container. Rinse the slide thoroughly with water. Remove paraffin wax to reveal the surface.5. Observation and Imaging: Observe the slide surface. Focus the image on the slide and record a time-lapse or accelerated sequence highlighting the etched pattern.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before etching: Glass surface is smooth and transparent; wax-covered areas are intact.2. After acid treatment and washing: Exposed regions appear frosted or roughened, while wax-covered regions remain smooth and transparent, forming a clear pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrofluoric acid reacts with silicon dioxide (SiO2) in glass, forming soluble fluorosilicates and causing material removal. Paraffin wax acts as a protective mask, preventing acid contact. Thus, only unmasked areas are etched, producing a patterned surface.Core reaction: SiO2 + 6HF → H2SiF6 + 2H2O.VI. PrecautionsHydrofluoric acid is highly hazardous; this experiment is for demonstration only with strict safety controls. Avoid direct contact and dispose of waste properly.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the condensation of water vapor when warm, humid air flows over a cold surface, and to visually observe fog formation using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentFlat metal plate (aluminum or stainless steel), cooling source (ice pack or refrigerated plate), table, source of warm humid air (human breath or humidifier with gentle airflow), thermometer (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, timer or time-lapse function.III. Cool the plate using ice packs or refrigeration until its surface temperature is clearly lower than room temperature. Ensure the surface is clean and dry.2. Core Operation: Gently blow warm, humid air across the surface of the cold plate, or direct a low-speed humid airflow over it. Maintain a steady and gentle airflow without disturbing the plate.4. Recording: Continue the airflow while recording for several seconds to capture the gradual formation and evolution of the fog layer.5. Completion: Stop the airflow, end the recording, and allow the plate to warm naturally. Turn off and store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Granular Material Sliding on Steep and Shallow Roofs2. Subject: Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how roof slope affects the sliding behavior of snow or granular materials, and to understand the role of gravity and friction in roof design.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo model roofs of identical material and surface texture; support stand to hold roofs side by side; white granular material (simulating snow); spoon or shaker for sprinkling; camera for close-up observation.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Simulating Mineralization Formation of Body FossilsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulating Mineralization Formation of Body Fossils2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate the process of body fossil mineralization by observing how mineral-rich solution infiltrates a porous material and gradually hardens, helping students understand the basic mechanism of fossil formation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBeaker (transparent), porous sponge sample (dry and clean), calcium carbonate solution (prepared in advance), dropper or pipette, label and marker, camera or mobile device for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the dry porous sponge sample at the bottom of a clean, transparent beaker. Ensure the sponge is fully visible from the side.2. Solution Addition: Use a dropper to slowly add calcium carbonate solution drop by drop onto the sponge. Observe the solution seeping into the pores of the sponge until it is evenly moistened but not submerged.3. Standing and Recording: Keep the beaker undisturbed at room temperature. Set the camera to focus on the beaker and record using time-lapse photography to simulate a long-term process.4. Observation Period: Allow the sample to stand for an equivalent of 30 days (accelerated in video form). Do not move or disturb the beaker during this period.5. Final Observation: At the end of the standing period, observe and record changes in the sponge’s hardness, color, and structure.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sponge is soft, porous, and lightweight; the calcium carbonate solution is clear or slightly cloudy.2. During Infiltration: The solution gradually seeps into the sponge’s pores, darkening it slightly as liquid is absorbed.3. After Standing: The sponge becomes harder and heavier; white or light-colored mineral deposits may be visible within or on the surface, and the structure appears more rigid.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment simulates body fossil mineralization. In natural environments, mineral-rich water infiltrates the remains of organisms buried in sediments. Over long periods, dissolved minerals precipitate and fill the pores of organic material, gradually replacing or reinforcing the original structure. In this simulation, calcium carbonate solution represents mineral-rich groundwater, and the sponge represents porous biological remains, demonstrating the basic principle of fossil mineralization.VI. Experimental Notes1. Add the solution slowly to ensure full infiltration into pores.2. Keep the beaker stationary during the standing period.3. Time-lapse recording is used to represent long geological timescales and does not reflect real-time mineralization speed.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Simulation of body fossil mineralization through mineral infiltration and precipitation in porous material. Minimum assumptions: calcium carbonate solution represents mineral-rich groundwater; sponge represents porous biological remains; time-lapse accelerates long-term geological processes. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) static setup with beaker and dry sponge; (2) dropwise addition of solution causing visible seepage into pores; (3) accelerated standing period via time-lapse; (4) gradual visual change such as whitening and stiffening of sponge. Visibility constraints: camera remains focused on the beaker; changes must be visually continuous and causally linked to prior steps.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Peroxidase–Guaiacol Reaction with Rapid Initial BrowningI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Peroxidase–Guaiacol Catalytic Oxidation Reaction2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the catalytic action of horseradish peroxidase on the oxidation of guaiacol by hydrogen peroxide, understand enzyme-catalyzed reaction characteristics, and recognize the phenomenon of rapid initial browning followed by reaction slowdown.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass cuvette (1, optical grade), cuvette holder (optional), pipette or dropper, guaiacol solution (colorless to pale yellow), hydrogen peroxide solution (dilute, colorless), horseradish peroxidase solution, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry clear glass cuvette on a flat surface. Ensure it is transparent and free of stains.2. Reagent Addition (Substrate): Using a pipette, add an appropriate volume of guaiacol solution into the cuvette, followed by hydrogen peroxide. Gently mix by slight tilting to ensure uniform distribution. The solution should remain nearly colorless.3. Enzyme Addition (Core Operation): Hold the cuvette steady. Using a clean pipette, add a small amount of horseradish peroxidase solution into the cuvette.4. Mixing: Gently swirl the cuvette once or twice to mix the contents evenly, avoiding vigorous shaking.5. Observation: Record the reaction from the side of the cuvette. Observe the color change over time.6. Completion: After the color change stabilizes, stop swirling and place the cuvette upright for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mixed guaiacol and hydrogen peroxide solution is clear or very lightly colored.2. Immediately after enzyme addition: The solution rapidly turns brown, with the color deepening quickly in the first few seconds.3. After a short time: The rate of browning slows down noticeably, and the color change becomes gradual until it nearly stops.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHorseradish peroxidase acts as a biological catalyst, accelerating the oxidation of guaiacol by hydrogen peroxide. In this reaction, guaiacol is oxidized to a brown-colored product (tetraguaiacol). The rapid initial browning reflects high substrate availability and high reaction rate. As substrates are consumed and product accumulates, the reaction rate decreases, resulting in a visible slowdown of color development. This experiment demonstrates key characteristics of enzyme-catalyzed reactions, including specificity and changing reaction rate over time.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: enzyme-catalyzed oxidation demonstrated by the peroxidase–guaiacol reaction. Minimum assumptions include the presence of guaiacol and hydrogen peroxide as substrates, horseradish peroxidase as catalyst, and a transparent vessel allowing side-view observation.Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial setup shows a clear or lightly colored solution in a glass cuvette; (2) addition of peroxidase via pipette initiates the reaction; (3) immediately after gentle swirling, the solution rapidly turns brown; (4) after the initial burst, the rate of color deepening visibly slows and stabilizes. Visibility constraints: the side view must clearly show color intensity changes in the solution, and the sequence must preserve cause–effect order rather than exact real-time duration.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Fluorescently Stained DNA Bands Under Blue or UV Light After Gel ElectrophoresisI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Fluorescently Stained DNA Bands Under Blue or UV Light2. Subject: Biology – Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe DNA fragments separated by agarose gel electrophoresis through fluorescence under blue or UV light, understand the principle of DNA staining and fluorescence, and learn correct observation and documentation methods using a fixed-focus camera.II. Experimental EquipmentAgarose gel containing separated DNA fragments, fluorescent DNA stain (e.g., ethidium bromide or safe alternative), clear gel tray, transilluminator (blue light or UV), protective shield or goggles, camera or smartphone with tripod, darkened observation environment.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the transilluminator on a stable laboratory bench and turn it off. Put on protective goggles if using UV light. Ensure the agarose gel has been properly stained and is fully set in a clear tray.Placement: Carefully place the clear gel tray containing the agarose gel onto the center of the transilluminator surface, ensuring it lies flat and does not slide.Illumination: Turn on the blue or UV light source. Adjust shielding to protect eyes and skin while allowing clear observation of the gel surface.Observation and Imaging: Observe the gel directly from above. Distinct fluorescent bands should appear within the gel lanes. Position the camera directly above the gel, adjust framing, and fix the focus manually. Mount the camera on a tripod and start time-lapse or continuous recording if required.Completion: After observation and imaging, turn off the light source, remove the gel tray, and dispose of the gel according to laboratory safety guidelines. Power down and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before illumination, the agarose gel appears translucent with no visible bands.2. Under Blue or UV Light: Bright fluorescent DNA bands appear within the gel lanes against a darker background. Band positions remain stable during observation.3. Imaging State: With fixed camera focus, the recorded images remain sharp and consistent over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDNA fragments migrate through agarose gel during electrophoresis based on size. Fluorescent dyes bind to DNA molecules. When excited by blue or UV light, these dyes emit visible fluorescence, allowing DNA bands to be visualized. The intensity and position of the bands reflect the amount and size of DNA fragments.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid direct exposure to UV light. Ensure the gel tray is transparent and clean. Do not move the gel during observation to maintain band clarity. Fix camera focus before recording to avoid image fluctuation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop ConsonantI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop ConsonantSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Linguistics - PhoneticsExperiment Objective: To observe and compare acoustic differences between a sustained vowel and a stop consonant using live spectrogram visualization, and to understand how articulatory properties are reflected in acoustic patterns.II. Experimental EquipmentComputer with phonetic analysis software capable of real-time spectrogram display (such as Praat), external microphone, microphone stand, quiet room, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse or continuous recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Open the phonetic analysis software and set the spectrogram to display time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis. Adjust microphone input levels to avoid clipping. Fix the camera focus to include the speaker, microphone, and spectrogram screen.Core Operation Step 1 (Vowel): The speaker positions their mouth close to the microphone and sustains a single vowel sound (such as a) steadily for several seconds while the spectrogram is displayed live.Pause: The speaker stops phonation briefly, remaining silent to create a clear separation in the spectrogram.Core Operation Step 2 (Stop Consonant): The speaker produces a stop consonant (such as p or t) once or twice into the microphone.Completion: Stop recording and save the spectrogram image or video for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Sustained Vowel: The spectrogram shows continuous, stable horizontal dark bands (formants) indicating steady resonance and voicing.2. Pause: The spectrogram shows a brief region of low energy or silence.3. Stop Consonant: The spectrogram shows a closure interval with little or no energy, followed by a sudden vertical burst indicating the release of the stop.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSpeech sounds have distinct acoustic signatures. Sustained vowels are produced with an open vocal tract and continuous vocal fold vibration, resulting in stable formant structures on the spectrogram. Stop consonants involve complete closure in the vocal tract, causing a period of silence, followed by a rapid release burst. Spectrogram visualization maps these articulatory differences into observable acoustic patterns over time and frequency.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Acoustic differentiation of vowels and stop consonants as visualized by a real-time spectrogram. Minimum assumptions: a functioning microphone, live spectrogram software, and a fixed camera view showing both speaker action and visualization. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 shows setup with stable framing and active spectrogram; Phase 2 shows sustained vowel production causing steady horizontal formant bands; Phase 3 shows a brief silent pause with reduced energy; Phase 4 shows stop consonant production with closure and burst patterns. Visibility constraints: the spectrogram must be readable, and timing between speech actions and visual changes must be directly observable for verification.

Experiment Title: Laser Pointer Scattering in a Milk–Water Tank with Increasing Particle Concentration2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how increasing particle concentration in a medium enhances light scattering, simulating atmospheric aerosol scattering, and to visually observe the change in laser beam visibility as milk particles are added to water.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent rectangular tank or glass aquarium (1), clean water, whole milk, dropper or measuring spoon, red laser pointer, tripod or fixed mount for laser, camera or smartphone with tripod (focus lock enabled), stirring rod or spoon, darkened room or shaded environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent tank on a stable table and fill it with clear water to about 3/4 full. Darken the room slightly to improve laser visibility. Initial Observation: Turn on the laser pointer and observe the beam path through the clear water. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Lucas Test – Reactivity of tert-Butanol vs EthanolSubject: Chemistry – Organic ChemistryObjective: To compare the reactivity of tertiary and primary alcohols with Lucas reagent through visual observation of turbidity formation, and to understand the SN1/SN2 reaction principles of alcohol substitution.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Copper Pipe Sleeve Joint Brazed with Silver Filler by Capillary ActionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper Pipe Sleeve Joint Brazed with Silver Filler by Capillary Action2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering (Manufacturing Processes / Joining Technology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the brazing process of a copper sleeve joint using silver-based filler metal, observe the capillary flow of molten filler into the joint clearance, and understand the basic principle of brazing and capillary action through visual time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials- Copper pipes (2 pieces, matching diameter, clean and deburred)- Copper sleeve (1 piece, appropriate clearance fit)- Silver brazing rod (silver-based filler metal)- Flux suitable for silver brazing of copper- Gas torch (propane or oxy-acetylene with appropriate flame setting)- Heat-resistant work surface or firebrick- Clamp or fixture (optional, for alignment)- Safety goggles, heat-resistant gloves- Camera on tripod (focus fixed, time-lapse mode enabled)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Wear safety goggles and heat-resistant gloves.   - Clean the outer surface of one copper pipe end and the inner surface of the sleeve using abrasive cloth to remove oxide and grease.   - Apply a thin, even layer of brazing flux to the cleaned surfaces.2. Assembly Stage:   - Insert the cleaned copper pipe into the sleeve to form a sleeve joint with uniform clearance.   - Ensure the joint is straight and stable; place it on a heat-resistant surface.   - Position the camera on a tripod, frame the joint clearly, fix focus manually, and start time-lapse recording.3. Heating Stage:   - Ignite the torch and adjust to a neutral flame.   - Heat the sleeve joint evenly by moving the flame around the circumference, focusing mainly on the sleeve rather than the filler rod.   - Continue heating until the flux becomes transparent and active, indicating suitable brazing temperature.4. Brazing Stage:   - Gently touch the tip of the silver brazing rod to the seam between the sleeve and pipe without directly melting it with the flame.   - Allow the heat of the joint to melt the filler; observe the molten silver filler being drawn into the joint by capillary action.5. Completion Stage:   - Once a visible fillet forms around the joint and filler has flowed through the seam, remove the brazing rod and torch.   - Allow the joint to cool naturally without disturbance.   - Stop the time-lapse recording after cooling.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The copper pipe and sleeve appear clean, metallic, and solid; flux is opaque or paste-like.2. During Heating: Flux melts and turns clear; copper surface darkens slightly due to heat.3. During Brazing: When the brazing rod contacts the hot seam, silver filler melts and rapidly flows into the joint gap, forming a bright, smooth ring along the seam.4. After Cooling: The joint shows a continuous silver-colored fillet around the sleeve, indicating successful brazing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBrazing is a metal-joining process in which a filler metal with a melting point lower than the base metals is melted and drawn into a close-fitting joint by capillary action. In this experiment, heating raises the copper joint above the melting temperature of the silver filler but below that of copper. Proper joint clearance and surface cleanliness allow molten silver filler to flow into the seam due to surface tension and wetting forces, forming a strong metallurgical bond upon cooling.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure all copper surfaces are thoroughly cleaned to promote proper wetting.2. Heat the joint evenly; do not overheat or directly melt the filler with the flame.3. Maintain a safe distance from the flame and hot metal; allow sufficient cooling time before handling.4. Fix camera focus before heating to ensure clear time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Silver brazing of a copper sleeve joint driven by capillary action. Minimum assumptions include clean copper surfaces, close-fitting sleeve joint, filler with lower melting point than copper, and uniform heating.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase – two copper pipes assembled into a sleeve joint, camera fixed and focused. (2) Heating phase – torch heats joint evenly, flux activates. (3) Brazing phase – silver filler contacts seam, melts from joint heat, and is drawn into gap by capillary action. (4) Completion phase – continuous silver fillet visible as joint cools. Visibility Constraints: Joint seam must remain in frame, filler flow visible along circumference, and time-lapse acceleration preserves correct chronological order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Beam Bridge Model Progressively Loaded with Small WeightsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Progressive Loading of a Simply Supported Beam Bridge Model2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the deformation behavior of a simply supported beam bridge under gradually increasing central load, understand the relationship between load and deflection, and illustrate basic concepts of structural mechanics through visual time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentSimply supported beam bridge model (rectangular beam), two rigid piers/supports, identical small weights (e.g., metal washers or calibrated masses), flat tabletop, ruler or deflection scale (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, fixed-focus setting, good ambient lighting.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the two rigid piers on a stable tabletop with a fixed span. Rest the beam horizontally on the piers to form a simply supported bridge. Ensure the beam is centered and initially unloaded. Set up the camera on a tripod facing the side of the beam, adjust framing to include the entire span, and lock focus and exposure for time-lapse photography.Initial Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording before applying any load, capturing the undeformed state of the beam.Progressive Loading: Place one identical small weight gently at the center of the beam deck. Wait briefly for the beam to stabilize, then place the next identical weight at the same central position. Repeat this process, adding weights one by one, keeping their position consistent and aligned.Termination: Stop adding weights when a clearly visible deflection is observed or before any damage occurs. End the recording.Cleanup: Carefully remove the weights, dismantle the setup, and store all equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The beam is straight and horizontal with no visible deflection.2. During Progressive Loading: With each added weight, the beam shows an increasing downward deflection at the center while remaining supported at both piers.3. Overall Trend: The deflection increases gradually and cumulatively as more identical weights are added, with the maximum deflection occurring at mid-span.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the fundamental principle of beam bending in structural engineering. A simply supported beam subjected to a concentrated load at mid-span experiences bending moments that cause elastic deformation. As the load increases, internal stresses and bending moments increase, resulting in greater deflection. Within the elastic range, the relationship between load and deflection is approximately linear, illustrating basic load–deflection behavior of beam structures.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: elastic bending behavior of a simply supported beam under incremental central loading. Minimum assumptions: rigid supports, identical weights, elastic beam, gravity-dominated response. Phased storyline: (1) undeformed beam on two piers; (2) first central weight causes slight mid-span deflection; (3) successive identical weights increase deflection step by step; (4) final state shows maximum visible deflection at center. Visibility constraints: side view with fixed focus to clearly compare deflection changes over time; no camera movement to ensure verifiable time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Infrared Observation of Asphalt Pavement vs Grass Lawn HeatingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Heating Comparison of Asphalt Pavement and Grass Lawn Under Direct Sunlight (Infrared View)2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To compare the heating characteristics of asphalt pavement and grass lawn under direct midday sunlight using an infrared camera, and to understand how surface properties influence temperature and near-surface thermal environment.II. Experimental EquipmentFixed infrared thermal imaging camera (with tripod), visible-light reference camera (optional), stopwatch or timer, open outdoor area with adjacent asphalt pavement and grass lawn, data recording sheet or device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Site Preparation: Select an outdoor location where dark asphalt pavement and green grass lawn are directly adjacent and fully exposed to midday sunlight. Ensure both surfaces are dry and unobstructed.2. Camera Setup: Mount the infrared camera on a tripod at a fixed position. Frame both surfaces in the same field of view, with asphalt on the left and grass on the right. Fix focus, angle, and thermal range; do not adjust during the experiment.3. Initial Recording: Start the infrared recording or time-lapse capture at the beginning of the observation period. Record the initial surface temperature distribution of both materials.4. Continuous Observation: Allow the camera to record continuously or at fixed intervals for a short, accelerated time-lapse period representing heating over time.5. Completion: Stop recording after a clear temperature contrast has developed. Save and label the recorded data.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At the start, both asphalt and grass show relatively moderate temperatures, with asphalt slightly warmer.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAsphalt has low albedo and high heat capacity, absorbing and storing more solar radiation, which leads to rapid temperature increase. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Effect of Selenium on Antioxidation (Simulation)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Selenium on Antioxidation (Simulation)Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneObjective: To visually demonstrate the antioxidant effect of selenium by comparing the oxidation rate of hydrogen peroxide in the presence of different selenium doses using a lipid oxidation indicator.II. Materials and ReagentsTest tubes (3 identical tubes), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration), lipid oxidation indicator (e.g., colorimetric oxidation indicator), selenium solution (low concentration and high concentration), timer or simulated time-lapse recording setup.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place three clean test tubes on a rack and label them Tube 1 (No Selenium), Tube 2 (Low Selenium), Tube 3 (High Selenium).2. Addition of Substrate: Using a pipette, add equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide solution to each test tube.3. Indicator Addition: Add the same number of drops of lipid oxidation indicator to each tube and gently swirl to mix.4. Selenium Treatment: Add no selenium to Tube 1; add a low-dose selenium solution to Tube 2; add a higher-dose selenium solution to Tube 3.5. Mixing and Placement: Gently mix all tubes to ensure uniform distribution. Place them side by side on the rack.6. Observation: Record or simulate a time-lapse observation, focusing the camera on the three tubes simultaneously to compare changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: All three tubes show the same indicator color immediately after mixing.Over Time: Tube 1 gradually shows the fastest and strongest color change indicating oxidation; Tube 2 shows a slower and weaker color change; Tube 3 shows the slowest or minimal color change.Comparative Result: The degree of oxidation decreases as selenium concentration increases.V. Experimental Principle SummarySelenium is an essential trace element involved in antioxidant defense, mainly as a component of selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidase. In this simulation, hydrogen peroxide represents an oxidative system, and the lipid oxidation indicator visually reflects oxidation intensity. Selenium enhances antioxidant activity, promoting the decomposition of peroxides and reducing oxidative reactions. Therefore, higher selenium concentrations result in slower oxidation and weaker indicator color changes.VI. Notes and PrecautionsEnsure equal volumes and identical conditions for all tubes except selenium dose. This experiment is a simulation for teaching purposes; time-lapse is used to accelerate observable differences.

Phase 3 (Time-lapse Reaction) – oxidation progresses fastest in the no-selenium tube, slower with low selenium, and slowest with high selenium. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk‑Diluted Water (Tyndall Scattering)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk‑Diluted Water (Tyndall Scattering)2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science (Optical properties of seawater)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the visibility of a laser beam in clear water and milk‑diluted water, understand the Tyndall scattering phenomenon caused by suspended particles, and recognize how particle concentration affects light propagation in marine environments.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical transparent tanks or glass containers2. Clear water (one tank filled)3. Milk‑diluted water (few drops of milk mixed evenly with water until slightly cloudy)4. Narrow green laser pointer (continuous beam)5. Stable stand or clamp for fixing the laser at a constant height6. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time‑lapse or continuous recording)7. Darkened room or shaded background (recommended for clear observation)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical transparent tanks side by side on a level surface. Fill one tank with clear water and the other with evenly mixed milk‑diluted water. Ensure both tanks have the same water level.2. Laser Setup: Fix the green laser pointer on a stand so that the beam can pass horizontally through both tanks at the same height, approximately through the middle of the water column.3. Camera Setup: Place the camera in front of the tanks, adjust framing so both tanks are fully visible, and fix the focus and exposure to avoid automatic changes during recording.4. Core Operation: Turn on the laser and slowly sweep or align the narrow green beam horizontally so it passes through the clear‑water tank first and then the milk‑diluted tank.5. Recording and Observation: Record continuously or using time‑lapse while keeping the laser height and camera position unchanged.6. Completion: Turn off the laser, stop recording, and clean up the equipment after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Clear Water Tank: The laser beam path inside the clear water is barely visible; only the entry and exit points on the tank walls can be clearly seen.2. Milk‑Diluted Water Tank: The laser beam path inside the water is clearly visible as a bright green line due to scattering by suspended milk particles.3. Comparison: Under identical conditions, the beam is significantly more visible in the milk‑diluted water than in the clear water.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the Tyndall scattering effect. Clear water contains very few suspended particles, so light passes through with minimal scattering, making the beam path invisible. Milk‑diluted water contains many tiny particles that scatter the laser light in multiple directions, allowing the beam path to be seen from the side. In marine science, this principle explains why light penetrates differently in clear ocean water versus turbid coastal or plankton‑rich water.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not shine the laser directly into eyes.2. Ensure milk is evenly mixed to avoid sediment affecting results.3. Keep laser height, tank position, and camera focus fixed to ensure a fair comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Tyndall scattering of light by suspended particles in water. Minimum assumptions: two identical transparent tanks, one containing clear water and the other containing uniformly milk‑diluted water; a narrow green laser travels horizontally at the same height through both tanks; camera focus and viewpoint remain fixed. Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial static setup with two tanks side by side; (2) Laser activation and horizontal beam entry into both tanks; (3) In clear water, the beam path remains mostly invisible; (4) In milk‑diluted water, the beam becomes a visible green line due to scattering; (5) Stable comparison view maintained. Verification requires a frontal or slight angled view that allows the side‑scattered light in the cloudy tank to be seen while maintaining consistent spatial alignment across time.

manual: Instructions for the Sport Demonstration: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip TurnI. Basic Experiment Information1. Title: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip Turn Demonstration2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Sport3. Objective: To demonstrate and understand the standard technical process of a freestyle forward flip turn, including approach, rotation, wall push-off, posture adjustment, and continuation of swimming.II. Experimental Environment and Equipment- Standard swimming pool with a clear wall and lane markings- Swimmer wearing standard swimwear and goggles- Underwater or side-view camera (optional, for observation)III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation: The athlete starts several meters away from the pool wall in a freestyle swimming posture, maintaining a steady rhythm.2. Approach: The athlete swims freestyle toward the wall, keeping the body horizontal and speed controlled.3. Head and Body Tuck: One arm finishes a stroke; the athlete lowers the head and initiates a forward rotation by tucking the chin toward the chest.4. Leg Tuck and Forward Flip: The knees are drawn toward the chest, forming a compact shape to complete a forward flip near the wall.5. Wall Contact and Push-off: Both feet contact the wall; the athlete forcefully pushes off, rotating the body to face the opposite direction.6. Posture Adjustment: After push-off, the athlete straightens into a streamlined position, aligns the body, and transitions back into freestyle.7. Continuation: The athlete resumes normal freestyle swimming away from the wall.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The swimmer approaches the wall smoothly without stopping.2. The head lowers and the body rotates forward in a compact flip.3. The feet clearly contact the wall, followed by a visible push-off.4. The swimmer glides briefly in a streamlined posture.5. Freestyle strokes resume in the opposite direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe freestyle forward flip turn is based on biomechanical and hydrodynamic principles. Forward momentum from swimming is converted into rotational motion by tucking the head and legs, reducing rotational inertia. A strong push-off from the wall generates propulsion in the opposite direction, while a streamlined posture minimizes water resistance, allowing efficient continuation of freestyle swimming.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet LampI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet LampSubject: Natural Science – Geology & GeophysicsExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the fluorescence phenomenon of minerals (calcite or fluorite) under ultraviolet (UV) illumination, and to master basic methods of controlled lighting observation and fixed-focus time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment1. Calcite or fluorite mineral specimen (clean, dry, visible crystal surface)2. Handheld ultraviolet lamp (long-wave UV recommended, ~365 nm)3. Stable table or flat surface4. Dark room or enclosure (lights fully off)5. Camera or smartphone with tripod (focus-lock or manual focus enabled)6. Tripod or fixed mount for UV lamp (optional)III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage:1. Place the mineral specimen at the center of a table in a dark room.2. Set up the camera on a tripod facing the mineral; adjust framing so the mineral remains fully in view.3. Manually focus the camera on the mineral surface and lock the focus to prevent refocusing during recording.4. Turn off all visible light sources to ensure a dark environment.Core Operation:5. Start video or time-lapse recording.6. Switch on the ultraviolet lamp and direct it steadily toward the mineral without changing distance or angle.7. Maintain illumination for several seconds to allow fluorescence to be clearly visible.8. Switch off the ultraviolet lamp while continuing recording.9. Repeat switching the UV lamp on and off once if needed, keeping all other conditions unchanged.Conclusion:10. Stop recording.11. Turn on room lights, turn off the UV lamp, and safely store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In darkness without UV light, the mineral appears dim or non-luminous.2. Under UV Illumination: When the ultraviolet lamp is switched on, the calcite or fluorite emits visible fluorescence, commonly appearing as blue, green, purple, or yellow glow.3. After UV Is Turned Off: The visible glow disappears immediately or rapidly, and the mineral returns to a dark appearance.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMineral fluorescence occurs when ultraviolet radiation excites electrons within impurity atoms or defects in the crystal lattice of certain minerals such as calcite or fluorite. These excited electrons absorb UV energy and then release part of that energy as visible light when returning to a lower energy state. The emitted visible light causes the mineral to glow only while exposed to ultraviolet radiation, demonstrating the fluorescence phenomenon.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct exposure of skin or eyes to ultraviolet light; do not look directly into the UV lamp.2. Keep camera focus and position fixed throughout the experiment to ensure valid comparison.3. Ensure complete darkness to improve visibility of fluorescence.4. Handle mineral specimens carefully to avoid damage.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Uneven Dye Spreading in Water vs OilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Uneven Dye Spreading in Water vs Oil2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how liquid polarity affects mass transfer and diffusion by observing the different spreading behaviors of food coloring in water and cooking oil.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass containers, water, cooking oil, food coloring, dropper, flat stable surface, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass containers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of water into one container and cooking oil into the other.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the containers, ensure both containers are fully in frame, fix focus and exposure, and enable time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, simultaneously release one drop of food coloring into the center of each container.4. manual: Experiment Title: Simulated Sedimentation and Burial in a JarSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyObjective: To demonstrate how sediment carried by water settles as water slows, gradually burying objects and forming layers, illustrating a key archaeological sedimentation process.Equipment: Clear glass jar with lid; clean water; mixed sediment (sand, silt, clay); small stones or beads; table; camera or phone with time-lapse function.Procedure: (1) Preparation: Place small stones at the bottom of the clear jar. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Causes Visible Forearm Muscle ContractionSubject: Healthcare – Occupational TherapyObjective: To demonstrate that neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) applied to the volar forearm can activate motor nerves and produce visible muscle contractions, and to document the phenomenon using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Left Image Setup (Advection Fog): Display a sea surface with arrows indicating horizontal wind. Show warm, moist air moving steadily over a colder sea surface.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin E Detection by Phosphomolybdic Acid Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Vitamin E Detection (Phosphomolybdic Acid Colorimetric Method)Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To detect the presence of vitamin E in vegetable oil extract through a colorimetric reaction with phosphomolybdic acid and to understand its redox-based detection principle.II. Experimental Reagents and EquipmentVegetable oil extract, phosphomolybdic acid ethanol solution, test tube, dropper, test tube rack, beaker, boiling water bath, heat source, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the test tube rack and wear protective gloves and goggles.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper or pipette to add 2 mL of vegetable oil extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add exactly 2 drops of phosphomolybdic acid ethanol solution into the test tube and gently shake to mix.4. Heating: Place the test tube into a boiling water bath and heat for approximately 1 minute.5. Completion: Remove the test tube from the water bath and place it back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The vegetable oil extract is light yellow and transparent or slightly turbid.During Heating: After heating with phosphomolybdic acid, the solution gradually develops a blue or blue-green coloration.Final State: The appearance of a distinct blue tone indicates the presence of vitamin E in the sample.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhosphomolybdic acid is a strong oxidizing agent. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Paper Chromatography of Black Marker InkI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Paper Chromatography of Black Marker Ink Using Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the separation of components in black marker ink using paper chromatography, understand capillary action and differential solubility, and learn basic chromatographic operation and observation methods.II. Experimental EquipmentWhite filter paper strip (one strip, about 2×10 cm), black water-soluble marker, clear container or beaker, clean water (as solvent), clip or tape (optional), camera or phone for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut a strip of white filter paper. Use a black marker to draw a small dot about 1–2 cm from the bottom edge of the paper. Allow the ink to dry.2. Solvent Setup: Pour a small amount of clean water into a clear container. The water level should be below the marker dot.3. Placement: Place the filter paper upright in the container so that its lower edge touches the water, ensuring the marker dot does not touch the water directly.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position to record a time-lapse of the experiment.5. Development: Allow the water to rise up the filter paper naturally. Do not disturb the setup.6. Completion: When the water front reaches near the top of the paper and color separation is visible, remove the paper and allow it to dry.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The filter paper is white with a single black marker dot near the bottom.2. During Development: Water slowly moves upward along the paper. The black ink spreads and gradually separates into several colored bands (such as blue, green, or yellow).3. Final State: Distinct color bands appear at different heights on the paper, showing separation of ink components.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePaper chromatography separates mixtures based on differences in solubility and adsorption. Water moves upward through the filter paper by capillary action, carrying soluble ink components. Different pigments travel at different speeds depending on their solubility in water and their attraction to the paper, resulting in visible separation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use water-soluble marker ink; permanent markers may not separate.2. Ensure the marker dot is above the water level at the start.3. Keep the setup stable and avoid shaking during development.4. Maintain fixed camera focus for clear time-lapse recording.
