manual: Instructions for the Experiment Thermal Convection Phenomenon Demonstration Experiment (Smoke Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermal Convection Phenomenon Demonstration (Smoke Method)2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the phenomenon of thermal convection in air by observing the motion of incense smoke when air at the bottom of a beaker is heated, and to understand that heated air becomes less dense and rises, forming an upward airflow.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass beaker (transparent, medium size), incense stick (1 piece), matches or lighter, glass slide (slightly larger than the beaker opening), alcohol lamp, alcohol (fuel), heat-resistant mat, tweezers or forceps (optional), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the beaker upright on a heat-resistant mat. Put on safety goggles. Prepare the alcohol lamp with alcohol and ensure it is stable.2. Smoke Source Placement: Light the incense stick and allow it to burn steadily. Place the lit incense vertically at the bottom center of the beaker so that smoke can rise freely inside the beaker.3. Covering the Beaker: Carefully place a glass slide over the mouth of the beaker, leaving no large gaps, so the air inside the beaker is relatively enclosed while still allowing observation.4. Heating Operation: Light the alcohol lamp and gently heat the bottom of the beaker directly beneath the incense.5. Observation: Observe the movement of the incense smoke inside the beaker during heating.6. Ending the Experiment: After clear smoke movement is observed, remove the alcohol lamp, extinguish it, and allow the apparatus to cool before removing the glass slide and incense.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before heating, the incense smoke rises slowly and irregularly, spreading gently inside the beaker.2. During Heating: When the bottom of the beaker is heated, the smoke above the heated region clearly moves upward in a concentrated stream, forming a visible upward airflow.3. After Heating Stops: When heating is stopped, the upward motion of smoke gradually weakens and returns to a slower, less organized motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates thermal convection in gases. When the air at the bottom of the beaker is heated by the alcohol lamp, its temperature increases, causing it to expand and decrease in density. The less dense hot air rises, while cooler, denser air moves downward to replace it, forming a convection current. The incense smoke acts as a tracer, making the upward movement of hot air visible. This confirms that heat transfer in fluids can occur through convection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle the alcohol lamp carefully and keep flammable materials away.2. Do not touch the beaker or glass slide during or immediately after heating to avoid burns.3. Ensure the experiment is conducted in a well-ventilated area.4. Extinguish the incense and alcohol lamp properly after the experiment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Water Erosion on a Soil Slope Under Simulated RainfallI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Erosion on a Soil Slope Under Simulated Rainfall2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the process of water erosion on a soil slope under rainfall conditions, identify runoff formation and sediment transport, and explain how rainfall intensity and slope contribute to soil erosion.II. Experimental Equipment1. Rectangular tray or shallow box2. Loose, dry soil (sieved, free of stones)3. Support block or stand (to tilt the tray)4. Watering can or spray bottle (to simulate steady rainfall)5. Clear container or beaker (to collect runoff)6. Camera or mobile phone fixed on a tripod (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the tray evenly with loose soil and gently level the surface. Place one end of the tray on a support block to form a gentle slope.2. Setup: Position a clear container at the lower end of the tray to collect runoff water and eroded soil. Fix the camera in front of the setup, ensuring the entire slope and container are in view, and lock the focus for time-lapse photography.3. Simulation of Rainfall: Use the watering can or spray bottle to apply steady, uniform rainfall from above the slope. Maintain a consistent height and flow rate.4. Observation Process: Continue rainfall for a short, continuous period while recording. Do not disturb the soil during the experiment.5. Completion: Stop the rainfall, end the recording, and observe the collected runoff and changes on the slope surface.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The soil surface is intact, loose, and dry, with no visible channels.2. During Rainfall: Water infiltrates the soil, then begins to flow downslope as surface runoff. Fine soil particles are carried by the flowing water.3. Later Stage: Small rills or channels form on the slope surface. The water collected in the container becomes muddy, indicating sediment transport.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates water erosion caused by rainfall on a soil slope. When rainfall exceeds the soil’s infiltration capacity, surface runoff forms. Gravity drives the runoff downslope, where flowing water detaches and transports soil particles. Over time, this process creates erosion features such as rills and results in sediment accumulation at the slope base.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Apply rainfall evenly to avoid artificial disturbances.2. Ensure the camera remains fixed and focused throughout recording.3. Avoid overly steep slopes that may cause sudden soil collapse.4. Experiment Objective: To observe the charging process of a capacitor in an RC series circuit through the gradual change in LED brightness; to understand the time-dependent behavior of current and voltage in an RC circuit; to relate electrical theory to visible phenomena.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (DC power supply, e.g., 3–9 V), switch, resistor (current-limiting, e.g., 220–1k ohm), capacitor (electrolytic, e.g., 100–1000 µF), LED, connecting wires, breadboard or workbench setup, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all components on the workbench. Ensure the camera is fixed, focused on the circuit, and remains stationary for time-lapse photography.2. Circuit Assembly: Connect the battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, and LED in series. Ensure correct LED polarity (anode to positive) and correct capacitor polarity.3. Initial State Check: Keep the switch open. Confirm the LED is off and the capacitor is uncharged.4. Core Operation: Flip the switch by hand to connect the battery to the circuit.5. Observation Stage: Maintain the switch in the closed position while recording. Observe the LED brightness change over time.6. Ending Operation: After the LED brightness stabilizes, stop recording. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the charging behavior of a capacitor in an RC circuit. When the switch is closed, the capacitor begins to charge through the resistor. Initially, the current is relatively large, causing the LED to emit light. As the capacitor charges, the voltage across it increases, reducing the current in the circuit. The LED brightness changes correspondingly until the capacitor is nearly fully charged and the circuit reaches a steady state. The process follows an exponential law characterized by the time constant τ = RC.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct polarity of the LED and capacitor to avoid damage.2. Experiment Objective: To observe diffraction and interference of water waves by using a shallow water wave tank with a barrier containing two narrow slits, and to understand the principle of wave superposition.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Incense Smoke Rising Faster Above a Warm Surface Than a Cold SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Incense Smoke Rise Above Warm and Cold Metal Surfaces2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that air heated by a warm surface rises faster than air above a cold surface, through visual comparison of incense smoke motion; to understand the role of temperature differences in air density and convection; to practice controlled observation using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentLit incense stick (1), incense holder, two identical flat metal plates (same size and material), heating source (electric hot plate or warm water bath), cooling source (ice pack or chilled metal block), heat-resistant mat, infrared thermometer or hand-held thermometer (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod (capable of time-lapse recording), fireproof surface, safety gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:Place the two identical metal plates horizontally on a fireproof surface, leaving a gap of about 10–15 cm between them. Ensure both plates are clean and dry. Mount the camera on a tripod facing the plates, adjust framing so both plates and the space above them are clearly visible, and fix the focus and exposure.2. Temperature Setup:Heat one metal plate evenly using the heating source until it is clearly warmer than room temperature (do not overheat). Place the cooling source under or in contact with the second plate so it becomes noticeably cooler than room temperature. Confirm that one plate is warm and the other cold.3. Incense Placement:Light the incense stick and wait until it produces a steady stream of smoke. Place the incense holder midway between the two plates so that the incense tip is centered, with smoke able to rise freely above both surfaces without obstruction.4. Core Operation and Recording:Start the time-lapse or continuous video recording. Do not move the camera or the plates during recording. Allow the incense to burn steadily for several seconds while smoke rises above both the warm and cold plates.5. Completion:After sufficient recording, stop the camera. Extinguish the incense safely. Turn off and remove the heating and cooling sources. Allow the plates to return to room temperature and clean the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State:Incense smoke rises gently upward from the incense tip, initially appearing similar on both sides.2. During Observation:Above the warm metal plate, the smoke column rises faster, becomes thinner, and disperses upward more quickly. Above the cold metal plate, the smoke rises more slowly, appears thicker, and may spread sideways or linger longer.3. Comparative Result:A clear difference in rising speed and vertical extent of smoke is visible between the warm-side air and the cold-side air.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates atmospheric convection caused by temperature differences. Air heated by the warm metal plate gains thermal energy, expands, becomes less dense, and rises more rapidly. Air above the cold plate remains cooler, denser, and rises more slowly. Incense smoke acts as a visible tracer of air motion, allowing direct observation of convection currents. This principle explains many atmospheric phenomena, such as thermal updrafts and air circulation near Earth’s surface.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the two metal plates are identical to avoid material-related differences.2. Keep the camera focus and position fixed throughout the experiment.3. Avoid drafts or air currents in the room that could disturb the smoke.4. Handle hot plates and lit incense carefully to prevent burns or fire hazards.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Thermal convection in near-surface air, assuming warmer air is less dense and rises while cooler air is denser and rises more slowly. Minimum assumptions include identical plate materials, clear temperature contrast, and smoke acting as a passive tracer. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) both plates static, incense produces steady smoke; (2) air above warm plate heats, creating an updraft that accelerates smoke upward; (3) air above cold plate remains relatively stable, slowing smoke rise; (4) sustained contrast visible over time. Visibility constraints: camera must remain fixed, both plates and smoke columns simultaneously visible, and no external airflow interfering with observation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sulfonamide Antibiotic Residue Detection in Milk (Test Strip Method)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Sulfonamide Antibiotic Residue Detection in Milk (Test Strip Method)Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneObjective: To qualitatively detect the presence or absence of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk using a rapid test strip method, and to understand the basic principle of competitive immunochromatographic detection.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentMilk sample (prepared liquid sample), sulfonamide antibiotic test strip, disposable dropper, timer or stopwatch, standard color card (provided with test strip kit).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sulfonamide test strip on a clean, flat surface. Ensure the milk sample has been pretreated according to kit instructions and is at room temperature.2. Sample Addition: Use the dropper to draw an appropriate amount of prepared milk sample solution. Carefully add the sample dropwise onto the reaction area of the test strip.3. Reaction Waiting: Start the timer immediately after adding the sample. Allow the test strip to react for the specified short time (usually 3–5 minutes; in demonstration, accelerated time-lapse is used).4. Result Comparison: After the reaction time, compare the color or line intensity on the test strip with the standard color card.5. Judgment: Determine whether sulfonamide residues are present or absent based on the comparison result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The test strip is dry, with no visible color development.2. During Reaction: After sample addition, the reaction area gradually shows color development or line formation.3. Final Result: The color or test line intensity is compared with the standard card; differences indicate negative or positive sulfonamide residue presence.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the principle of immunochromatography. Sulfonamide residues in the milk sample compete with labeled antigens on the test strip for antibody binding sites. If sulfonamide residues are present above the detection limit, the test line color weakens or disappears; if absent, a clear test line appears. The result is determined by visual comparison with a standard color card, enabling rapid qualitative screening of antibiotic residues in food.VI. PrecautionsEnsure correct sample volume is added; do not touch the reaction area; read results within the specified time window; dispose of used strips properly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Rapid qualitative detection of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk using a test strip based on immunochromatographic competition.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Milk sample is properly prepared; test strip functions normally; added sample migrates along the strip by capillary action; color development reflects antibody–antigen interaction.Phased Storyline:Phase 1 – Setup: Milk sample, test strip, dropper, timer, and color card are clearly presented in frame.Phase 2 – Action: Sample solution is added to the strip reaction area using a dropper.Phase 3 – Reaction: Time-lapse shows brief waiting period as color or lines develop on the strip.Phase 4 – Outcome: Strip is compared side-by-side with the standard color card to judge presence or absence.Visibility and Perspective Constraints: Camera remains focused on the strip reaction area; color changes and comparison card must be clearly visible; accelerated timing is acceptable as long as step order and causal logic are preserved.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparative Experiment of Bearing Capacity between Pile Foundation and Non-Pile Foundation under Seismic LoadI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Bearing Capacity between Pile Foundation and Non-Pile Foundation under Seismic LoadSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To compare the bearing capacity and seismic settlement performance of pile foundations and non-pile foundations through a simulated vibration experiment, and to understand the role of piles in improving foundation stability under seismic load.II. Experimental EquipmentSand table A (with three model piles installed vertically), sand table B (without piles), uniform sand, model piles, vibration table, two identical weights, fixing clamps or bolts, measuring scale or visual markers, camera for focused and time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill sand table A with sand and install three model piles evenly spaced; fill sand table B with the same type and amount of sand without piles. Level the sand surfaces.2. Loading: Place identical weights at the center of the surface of each sand table to ensure equal load conditions.3. Fixation: Secure both sand tables firmly onto the vibration table to prevent sliding or tilting during vibration.4. Vibration: Start the vibration table to simulate seismic loading. Maintain the same vibration intensity and duration for both sand tables.5. Observation: Use a focused camera and time-lapse recording to observe and compare the settlement of the weights in sand tables A and B during vibration.6. Completion: Stop vibration after sufficient settlement is observed. Record final settlement states and compare results.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both weights rest stably on the sand surfaces with no visible settlement difference.2. During Vibration: Settlement begins in both sand tables. The weight on sand table B (non-pile foundation) settles faster and deeper.3. Final State: Sand table A shows smaller settlement and better stability, while sand table B shows larger and more uneven settlement.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnder seismic load, vibration causes sand particles to rearrange and lose strength temporarily. In a non-pile foundation, the load is carried mainly by shallow soil, leading to significant settlement. In a pile foundation, piles transfer part of the load to deeper, more stable soil layers, reducing surface settlement and improving bearing capacity and seismic performance.

manual: Instructions for the Data Visualization Experiment: Comparing Strong and Weak Negative Correlation Scatter PlotsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Strong and Weak Negative Correlation Using Scatter Plots2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare strong and weak negative correlations by constructing two scatter plots on the same coordinate axes, observe how data point dispersion affects correlation strength, and understand the meaning of a trend line in correlation analysis.II. Experimental Tools and Materials- Coordinate axes (x–y plane) displayed on screen or graph paper- Dataset A: data with strong negative correlation- Dataset B: data with weak negative correlation- Scatter plot drawing tool or visualization software (e.g., spreadsheet or plotting interface)- Trend line (linear regression) fitting functionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Axes Setup: Draw or display a fixed set of x–y axes with labeled horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes. Keep the axes unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Strong Negative Correlation Plot:   a. Gradually add data points from Dataset A onto the axes, one by one.   b. Observe that as x increases, y clearly decreases.   c. After all points are added, fit a straight trend line through the points.3. Weak Negative Correlation Plot:   a. Clear only the data points but keep the same axes.   b. Gradually add data points from Dataset B onto the same axes.   c. Observe that as x increases, y shows a slight decreasing tendency but with large dispersion.   d. Fit a straight trend line through these points.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Strong Negative Correlation:   - Data points are closely clustered around a downward-sloping line.   - The negative trend is obvious and visually clear.   - The fitted trend line closely matches most data points.2. Weak Negative Correlation:   - Data points are widely scattered around the plot.   - The downward trend is subtle and not immediately obvious.   - The fitted trend line has a slight negative slope, but many points lie far from it.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCorrelation describes the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two variables. In a strong negative correlation, increases in one variable are consistently associated with decreases in the other, causing points to cluster near a downward trend line. In a weak negative correlation, although the overall direction is still downward, random variation dominates, resulting in points scattered far from the trend line. The trend line represents the average linear tendency of the data but does not imply perfect prediction.VI. Experimental Notes- The axes must remain the same to ensure a fair visual comparison.- Adding points step by step helps reveal how correlation strength emerges from data distribution.- The trend line summarizes overall tendency, not individual point accuracy.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: negative correlation strength and its visual interpretation in scatter plots. Minimum assumptions: fixed coordinate axes, two datasets with different dispersion but similar downward tendency, and a linear trend line summarizing data tendency. Expected phased storyline: (1) establish stable axes; (2) add points forming a clear downward cluster and fit a trend line to show strong negative correlation; (3) reset points while keeping axes; (4) add widely scattered points with a slight downward tendency and fit a trend line to show weak negative correlation. Key causal transition: increasing dispersion weakens visible correlation despite similar direction. Visibility constraints: points, axes, and trend lines must remain clearly visible throughout for comparison.

Experiment Title: Circular Drum Membrane Vibrating in One Normal Mode Pattern2. Subject: Physics – Waves and Vibrations3. Experiment Objective: To observe the normal mode vibration of a circular membrane by visualizing nodal patterns formed by fine sand under continuous fixed-frequency driving.II. Experiment Objective: To observe the reaction of sodium peroxide with water, verify oxygen generation and alkaline products, and understand the chemical principle of peroxide hydrolysis.II. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium peroxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide. The hydrogen peroxide further decomposes into water and oxygen. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scissor Linkage Lift Extending and Collapsing Vertically2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a scissor linkage mechanism converts rotational motion from a hand crank into vertical linear motion, and to observe the extending and collapsing behavior of the lift under controlled visual conditions suitable for time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Metal scissor linkage lift model (with base plate and top platform)2. Side-mounted hand crank connected to the linkage drive mechanism3. Flat, stable work surface4. Camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod (fixed focus and fixed position)5. Adequate lighting to clearly show linkage motionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the scissor linkage lift on a stable horizontal surface. Ensure the base plate is stationary and the top platform is unloaded. Set up the camera directly facing the side or front of the lift, fix the focus and framing, and do not move the camera during the experiment.2. Initial State Check: Confirm that the scissor linkage is in its lowest (collapsed) position and that all linkage arms are aligned symmetrically.3. Extension Operation: Slowly turn the side hand crank forward (clockwise). Continue rotating at a steady speed. Observe the scissor arms opening and the top platform rising vertically while remaining parallel to the base plate.4. Maximum Height Observation: Stop turning when the lift reaches its maximum designed height. Hold briefly to record the fully extended state.5. Collapse Operation: Turn the hand crank backward (counterclockwise) at a steady speed. Observe the scissor arms closing and the top platform descending vertically back toward the base plate.6. End State: Stop turning when the lift returns to its fully collapsed position. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The scissor linkage is compact, with crossed metal arms close together and minimal vertical distance between base and platform.2. During Forward Cranking: As the crank rotates forward, the crossed arms rotate about their pivot joints, extending outward and upward, causing a smooth vertical rise of the top platform.3. Fully Extended State: The linkage arms form a wider X-shape, and the top platform reaches its maximum height while remaining stable and level.4. During Reverse Cranking: Reversing the crank direction causes the arms to rotate back inward, and the top platform descends smoothly.5. Final State: The mechanism returns to its original collapsed configuration without lateral shift or sudden motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe scissor linkage lift operates on the principle of kinematic linkage transformation. Rotational motion applied through the hand crank is transmitted via a screw or gear mechanism to the scissor arms. The crossed arms rotate about pivot joints, constraining motion primarily to the vertical direction. As the linkage angle increases, vertical height increases; as the angle decreases, the lift collapses. This demonstrates the conversion of rotational input into controlled linear output, a fundamental concept in mechatronics and robotic mechanisms.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not overload the top platform to avoid deformation or instability.2. Turn the hand crank smoothly to prevent sudden jerks or damage to joints.3. Ensure fingers and loose clothing are kept away from moving linkage arms.4. Keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent visual comparison for time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate a scissor linkage lift mechanism that converts rotational hand-crank input into vertical linear motion, assuming rigid metal arms, pivot joints, a fixed base plate, and a level top platform.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: The linkage arms are identical and symmetrically arranged; pivot joints allow rotation without translation; the base plate is fixed; crank rotation directly drives linkage geometry change.Expected Phenomena – Phased Storyline:Phase 1 (Initial): Lift is fully collapsed; scissor arms are close together; camera view is fixed and stable.Phase 2 (Cause): Hand crank turns forward.Phase 3 (Effect): Scissor arms rotate outward; top platform rises vertically while staying level.Phase 4 (Transition): Crank stops at maximum extension; linkage holds height.Phase 5 (Cause): Hand crank turns backward.Phase 6 (Effect): Scissor arms rotate inward; top platform descends smoothly back to base.Visibility and Perspective Constraints: The entire scissor linkage, base plate, top platform, and hand crank must remain in frame; camera focus and position remain fixed to allow clear verification of vertical motion and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock PulseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock Pulse2. Subject: Engineering – Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic working principle of a digital shift register by visually observing how a row of LEDs changes state in response to visible clock pulses, and to grasp the relationship between clock signals, data input, and sequential logic.II. Experimental EquipmentShift register integrated circuit (e.g., 74HC595 or equivalent), LED array (8 LEDs) with current-limiting resistors, fixed data source (logic HIGH or LOW), clock button or rotary pulse knob, power supply (5V), breadboard and connecting wires.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power off the circuit. Insert the shift register IC into the breadboard. Connect the power and ground pins correctly. Connect each output pin of the shift register to an LED through a resistor.2. Data Setup: Connect the data input pin of the shift register to a fixed logic level (e.g., HIGH) so that identical data bits are shifted in each time.3. Clock Setup: Connect the clock input pin to a visible clock source, such as a push button or knob that generates single pulses when pressed or turned.4. Initial State: Power on the circuit and ensure all LEDs are initially off or in a known state.5. Core Operation: Use your hand to press the clock button or turn the knob repeatedly, generating one clock pulse at a time.6. Completion: After several pulses, observe the full shifting cycle, then power off the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All LEDs are off, or only the first LED is on, depending on the reset condition.2. During Clock Triggering: Each time the clock is triggered, the lit LED shifts one position along the row in a fixed direction.3. Repeated Triggering: With continuous clock pulses, the lit state propagates across the entire LED row, demonstrating sequential shifting.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA shift register is a sequential digital circuit composed of cascaded flip-flops. On each rising (or falling) edge of the clock signal, the data at the input is transferred to the first flip-flop, while the stored data in each flip-flop shifts to the next stage. The LEDs connected to the outputs visually represent the internal state of the register, making the effect of clock-driven data shifting directly observable.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct power polarity to avoid damaging the IC.2. Use appropriate resistors to protect LEDs from overcurrent.3. Trigger the clock slowly to make LED changes clearly visible.4. Power off the circuit before modifying connections.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: A digital shift register where a fixed data input is advanced step-by-step through internal flip-flops by discrete clock pulses. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Pre-charged and Uncharged Capacitors Driving an LEDSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate that a pre-charged capacitor can temporarily supply energy to drive an LED when a circuit is closed, and to compare its behavior with an uncharged capacitor under identical conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical LEDs, two identical resistors, two identical electrolytic capacitors, DC power supply (for pre-charging), single-pole switch (one switch controlling both branches), connecting wires, capacitor sleeves (red and blue), camera on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Assembly: Build two identical LED–resistor–capacitor branches side by side. Ensure correct LED polarity. Mark the left capacitor with a red sleeve and the right with a blue sleeve.2. Pre-charging: Disconnect the left (red) capacitor from the LED circuit. Connect it briefly to the DC power supply to fully charge it, then disconnect it from the supply.3. Initial State: Leave the right (blue) capacitor uncharged and disconnected from any power source. Ensure both branches are open at the switch.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse or continuous recording, ensuring both branches are clearly visible.5. Core Operation: Close the single switch to simultaneously connect both capacitor branches to their respective LEDs.6. Completion: Observe until LED brightness changes cease, then open the switch and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Moment: Upon closing the switch, the LED connected to the pre-charged red capacitor lights up immediately.2. Short-term Change: The brightness of this LED gradually decreases as the capacitor discharges through the resistor and LED.3. Comparison: The LED connected to the uncharged blue capacitor remains dark or shows only a negligible transient response.4. Final State: After a short time, both LEDs are off, and both capacitors are discharged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA capacitor stores electrical energy when charged. When connected to a load, it releases this stored energy, producing a transient current. In this experiment, the pre-charged capacitor discharges through the LED–resistor path, causing the LED to emit light briefly. The uncharged capacitor has no stored energy and therefore cannot drive the LED. The resistor limits current, and the LED brightness decay reflects the RC discharge process.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: A capacitor stores electrical energy and can act as a temporary power source; an uncharged capacitor cannot drive a load. Minimum assumptions: identical components, correct polarity, and simultaneous switching.Expected Phenomena Storyline: (1) Initial static setup with two identical branches visible; (2) switch closure as the causal trigger; (3) immediate LED illumination on the pre-charged side only; (4) gradual fading due to capacitor discharge; (5) stable dark state on the uncharged side throughout. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear view of LED brightness and capacitor color coding to verify causal comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Dissolving in Water Enables Electrical ConductionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salt Dissolving in Water Enables Electrical Conduction2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that pure water conducts electricity poorly, while salt dissolved in water forms ions that enable electrical conduction between electrodes.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers of the same size; table salt (sodium chloride); distilled or pure water; two identical pairs of metal electrodes; two identical simple circuits (battery, connecting wires, and small bulb or LED); stirring rod or spoon; camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two empty beakers side by side on a stable table. Ensure the camera is fixed, focused on both beakers and circuits, and will not move during recording.2. Liquid Setup: Pour equal volumes of pure water into both beakers. Label one as Pure Water and the other as Salt Solution.3. Salt Dissolution: Add a measured amount of salt to the Salt Solution beaker. Stir until the salt is completely dissolved and the solution is clear.4. Electrode Installation: Insert identical metal electrodes into each beaker, ensuring the electrodes do not touch each other and are immersed to the same depth.5. Circuit Connection: Connect each pair of electrodes to an identical circuit with a battery and bulb. Keep both circuits switched off initially.6. Core Operation: Simultaneously switch on both circuits while recording.7. Observation and Recording: Observe the brightness of the bulbs in both circuits over a short period. Maintain fixed camera focus for time-lapse capture.8. Completion: Switch off the circuits, remove electrodes, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before switching on, both bulbs are off; both liquids are clear and colorless.2. After Switching On: The bulb connected to the pure water beaker remains off or very dim. The bulb connected to the salt solution lights up clearly.3. Comparison: A clear brightness difference is observed between the two circuits.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPure water contains very few free ions and therefore has very low electrical conductivity. When salt (sodium chloride) dissolves in water, it dissociates into sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl−). These mobile ions move under the electric field between electrodes, carrying charge and enabling electrical current to flow, which lights the bulb.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Ionic conduction in aqueous solutions. Minimum assumptions: salt dissociates into ions in water; ions act as charge carriers; pure water has negligible conductivity. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – setup shows two identical circuits and clear liquids; Phase 2 – salt dissolves fully in one beaker; Phase 3 – circuits switched on; Phase 4 – bulb in salt solution lights while pure water bulb remains off or dim. Visibility constraints: both beakers, electrodes, bulbs, and brightness difference must be clearly visible in a fixed, stable frame.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Muddy Sediment Flow in a Clear Laboratory FlumeSubject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentology)Objective: To demonstrate how muddy sediment behaves in turbulent flowing water and how reduced flow velocity leads to sediment settling, simulating natural river deposition processes.II. Experimental EquipmentClear laboratory flume with transparent side walls; water circulation pump with adjustable flow rate; fine sediment or clay to prepare muddy water; water reservoir; flow control valve; fixed-position camera for side-view time-lapse recording; measuring scale on flume wall (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the flume with clean water and ensure all air bubbles are removed. Fix the camera perpendicular to the flume side, focusing on the full water column.2. High-Flow Operation: Start the pump and set a high flow rate to generate visible turbulence. Allow muddy water to circulate steadily.4. Observation Phase I: Record the turbulent flow; observe sediment remaining suspended throughout the water column.5. Flow Reduction: Gradually reduce the pump flow rate using the control valve.6. Observation Phase II: Continue recording as turbulence weakens and sediment begins to settle toward the flume bottom.7. Completion: Stop the pump after clear settling patterns are visible; save the time-lapse recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Clear flume with uniformly muddy water under strong turbulent flow.During high flow: Sediment remains suspended, giving the water a uniformly opaque appearance.After flow reduction: Turbulence decreases; sediment particles slowly descend, forming a clearer upper layer and sediment accumulation near the bottom.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates sediment transport and deposition principles. Under high flow velocity and turbulence, fine sediments are kept in suspension by upward fluid forces. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Starch–Iodine Color Change During Amylase Digestion of StarchI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Starch–Iodine Color Change During Amylase Digestion of Starch2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Biochemistry/Physiology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that amylase digests starch into smaller sugars, resulting in loss of the characteristic blue-black iodine–starch color, and to compare treated and untreated starch visually.II. Experimental EquipmentClear beakers (2), starch solution (cloudy, equal volumes), amylase solution, iodine solution, droppers, glass stirring rods or gentle swirling by hand, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place two clear beakers side by side on the lab bench. Add equal volumes of cloudy starch solution to each beaker. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse photography.Treatment Setup: Label the left beaker as experimental and the right as control. Add a measured amount of amylase solution to the left beaker only. Do not add amylase to the right beaker.Reaction and Testing: At regular intervals, gently swirl each beaker. Using a dropper, add 1–2 drops of iodine solution into each beaker while swirling to ensure mixing.Recording: Continue periodic iodine addition and swirling while recording the process with a fixed-focus time-lapse camera.Completion: Stop the experiment once a clear difference in color response between the two beakers is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain cloudy starch solution; upon iodine addition, both turn blue-black.During Digestion: Over time, the left beaker with amylase shows a gradual fading of the blue-black color after iodine addition.Control Comparison: The right beaker without amylase consistently turns blue-black when iodine is added.Final State: The experimental beaker shows little to no blue-black color, while the control remains dark blue-black.V. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heat Conduction Comparison of Metal, Wood, and Plastic Rods Using Wax DotsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparative Heat Conduction in Metal, Wood, and Plastic Rods2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the heat conduction abilities of different materials (metal, wood, plastic) by observing the melting sequence of wax dots when one end of each rod is heated simultaneously; to understand the concept of thermal conductivity and its relevance to engineering heat transfer.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal rod, wood rod, plastic rod (same length and diameter); wax (or small wax dots pre-attached at equal intervals along each rod); heat source (alcohol lamp or electric heater); retort stand or supports to keep rods horizontal; heat-resistant mat; stopwatch or timer; camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse photography; safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the three rods horizontally on supports so that they are parallel and aligned. Ensure one end of each rod extends equally toward the heat source. Attach small wax dots at equal distances along the length of each rod. Set up the camera facing the rods, adjust framing and focus, and lock the focus for time-lapse recording.2. Heating Setup: Position the heat source so that it can heat one end of all three rods simultaneously and uniformly. Place a heat-resistant mat beneath the setup.3. Core Operation: Start the camera time-lapse recording. Ignite or turn on the heat source and begin heating the aligned ends of the three rods at the same time. Maintain steady heating without moving the rods.4. Observation Stage: Allow heating to continue while observing the wax dots along each rod. Do not adjust the camera or rods during heating.5. Completion: After clear differences in wax melting are observed, turn off the heat source. Stop the recording after the key phenomena are captured. Allow the rods to cool before dismantling the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All wax dots on the three rods are solid and evenly spaced; rods are at room temperature.2. During Heating: On the metal rod, wax dots closest to the heated end melt first, followed by successive dots farther away. On the wood rod, wax dots melt slowly or only very near the heated end. On the plastic rod, wax dots melt minimally or may deform locally near the heat source.3. Final State: The metal rod shows the longest distance of melted wax dots, the wood rod shows limited melting, and the plastic rod shows the least effective heat transfer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat conduction, the transfer of thermal energy through a material due to a temperature gradient. Different materials have different thermal conductivities. Metals have high thermal conductivity, so heat travels quickly along the rod, melting wax farther from the heat source. Wood and plastic have much lower thermal conductivity, so heat transfer is slower and limited. In nuclear engineering and other engineering fields, understanding material heat conduction is essential for reactor design, thermal management, and safety analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal heating conditions for all rods.2. Fix the camera focus and position to maintain consistent visual records.3. Avoid touching heated rods directly; use protective equipment.4. Turn off the heat source promptly after observations are complete.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: comparative heat conduction based on material thermal conductivity. Minimum assumptions: three rods of equal geometry, identical heating at one end, wax as a visible phase-change indicator, and fixed camera perspective. Visibility constraints: rods must remain horizontal and fully in frame, wax dots clearly visible, and camera focus fixed to allow time-lapse verification of causal order.

Experiment Title: Infrared Thermal Camera Observation of a Warm Handprint on a Tabletop2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experimental EquipmentInfrared thermal camera (with video and time-lapse function), stable tripod, flat tabletop surface (wood or laminate preferred), room with stable ambient temperature, bare human hand, computer or storage device for saving images or video.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Linear Perspective Construction of a City StreetI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Linear Perspective Construction with a Single Vanishing Point2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Renaissance Painting)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the principle of linear perspective used in Renaissance painting by constructing a city street scene with a single vanishing point and orthogonal lines, and to visually understand how depth is represented on a flat surface.II. Experimental EquipmentDrawing paper or sketchbook, pencil and eraser, ruler or straightedge, drawing board or table, reference image of a city street (optional), camera mounted on a tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the paper flat on the drawing surface. Set up the camera on a tripod above or in front of the drawing area. Fix the camera focus and framing to remain unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Establish the Horizon Line: Using a ruler, lightly draw a horizontal line across the paper to represent the viewer’s eye level (horizon).3. Set the Vanishing Point: Mark a single point at the center of the horizon line. This will serve as the vanishing point.4. Draw the Foreground: Sketch the edges of the street and nearby buildings in the foreground, keeping vertical lines vertical.5. Pull Orthogonal Lines: From key points in the foreground (street edges, building bases, rooflines), draw straight lines using the ruler so that they converge toward the vanishing point.6. Define Depth and Details: Add windows, doors, and street elements, ensuring their horizontal edges follow the orthogonals toward the vanishing point.7. Final Observation: Stop drawing once the depth illusion is clear. End the time-lapse recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The paper is flat with no depth illusion before construction.2. During Construction: As orthogonal lines converge toward the vanishing point, the street and buildings begin to appear to recede into space.3. Final State: The completed drawing shows a convincing city street with strong depth, all spatial elements aligned to a single vanishing point.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLinear perspective is a geometric system developed during the Renaissance to represent three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface. When parallel lines receding into space are drawn to converge at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, the viewer perceives depth and distance. The horizon line represents eye level, and orthogonal lines guide the scaling of objects as they recede, creating a realistic spatial illusion.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the camera focus fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.2. Use a ruler for orthogonal lines to maintain geometric accuracy.3. Avoid adding multiple vanishing points, as this experiment focuses on single-point perspective.

Experiment Title: Measurement of Soil pH Using a Handheld pH Meter2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To measure and compare the pH values of acidic and alkaline soils, verify that acidic soil has pH<7 and alkaline soil has pH>7, and master the correct use of a handheld soil pH meter.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld soil pH meter (with probe), standard buffer solutions for calibration (pH 4.0 and/or pH 7.0), two soil samples (one acidic, one alkaline) placed in containers and clearly labeled, distilled water, spray bottle or dropper for moistening soil, clean tissue or cloth for probe cleaning.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Label two containers as acidic soil and alkaline soil. Lightly moisten each soil sample so it is damp but not waterlogged.2. Calibration: Turn on the handheld pH meter and calibrate it using standard buffer solution according to the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure accuracy.3. Measurement of Acidic Soil: Insert the clean probe vertically into the moist acidic soil. Ensure good contact between probe and soil. Wait until the reading stabilizes, then record the displayed pH value.4. Probe Cleaning: Remove the probe and rinse it with distilled water. Gently wipe it dry with a clean tissue.5. Measurement of Alkaline Soil: Insert the cleaned probe into the moist alkaline soil. Wait for the reading to stabilize and record the displayed pH value.6. Completion: Turn off the pH meter, clean the probe, and store all equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSoil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of soil, defined by the concentration of hydrogen ions. Experiment Title: Food Dye Diffusion Through Agar Gel with Pre-cut Channels2. Subject: Engineering - Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate molecular diffusion in a gel medium and observe how pre-cut channels influence transport paths, using food dye as a tracer.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear rectangular agar gel slab (transparent, with visible pre-cut straight channels), food dye (liquid, dark color such as blue or red), plastic dropper or pipette, flat table surface, camera or smartphone with tripod, adequate lighting.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Light Dispersion by a PrismI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Light Dispersion (Prism Light Splitting)2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe that white sunlight passing through a prism is dispersed into a band of seven colors, and to identify the distribution and order of these colors.II. Experimental EquipmentTriangular glass prism (one piece, clean and transparent), sunlight (direct sunlight near a window or outdoor sunlight), white screen or white paper (used to receive the spectrum), darkened room or shaded area (to improve contrast), prism stand or books (optional, for stabilizing the prism).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Choose a location where direct sunlight is available. Slightly darken the surrounding environment by closing curtains or turning off indoor lights to make the light band clearer. Place a white screen or white paper vertically or flat on a table.Prism Placement: Place the glass prism on a stable surface or prism stand near the sunlight source. Adjust the prism so that sunlight enters one face of the prism at an angle.Core Operation: Slowly rotate or tilt the prism until the refracted light emerging from the prism falls onto the white screen or paper.Observation: Carefully observe the light band formed on the screen. Adjust the prism angle if necessary until a clear and complete color band appears.Experiment Conclusion: Once the color band is clearly visible, fix the prism position and observe the color distribution and order. After observation, remove the prism and store the equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before the prism is placed in sunlight, the sunlight appears white and no color band is seen on the screen.2. During the Experiment: After sunlight passes through the prism, a long colored light band appears on the white screen.3. Final Observation: The light band is composed of seven distinct colors arranged in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. Red light deviates the least, while violet light deviates the most.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhite light is composed of light of different wavelengths. When white light passes through a prism, different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts due to the prism material having different refractive indices for different colors. This causes white light to spread out into a spectrum of seven colors, a phenomenon called dispersion.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly at the sun to avoid eye damage.2. Ensure the prism surfaces are clean to obtain a clear spectrum.3. Keep the prism stable during observation to prevent the spectrum from shaking or disappearing.

Experiment Objective: To observe the light emission phenomenon of a gas discharge tube under high voltage, understand gas ionization and excitation processes, and relate laboratory discharge phenomena to astronomical emission spectra.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed glass gas discharge tube (filled with low-pressure gas such as neon or argon), high-voltage power supply with adjustable voltage control, connecting wires with insulation, tube holder or stand, dark laboratory environment, safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the gas discharge tube securely on its holder in a darkened laboratory. Ensure all connections to the high-voltage power supply are correct and insulated. Wear safety goggles.2. Initial State: Confirm that the voltage control knob on the power supply is set to the off or minimum position and that the tube is not glowing.3. Core Operation: Turn off ambient lights. Slowly and steadily turn the voltage control from off toward a higher setting using one hand, observing the tube continuously.4. Observation: As the voltage increases, watch for the appearance and intensification of light inside the tube.5. Shutdown: After observation, turn the voltage control back to off, then restore room lighting and disconnect the power supply.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The gas discharge tube appears dark and transparent with no visible light emission.2. During Voltage Increase: A faint glow appears inside the tube, gradually becoming brighter as voltage increases. The glow may show characteristic colors depending on the gas.3. Stable Discharge: At sufficient voltage, the tube emits a steady, uniform glow along its length.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen high voltage is applied across the low-pressure gas in the sealed tube, free electrons are accelerated by the electric field and collide with gas atoms. These collisions excite or ionize the atoms. When excited atoms return to lower energy states, they emit light at characteristic wavelengths, causing the tube to glow. This principle is analogous to emission processes observed in astronomical nebulae and stellar atmospheres.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Never touch the tube or connections while power is on.2. Increase voltage gradually to avoid damaging the tube.3. Always turn the voltage to off before adjusting connections or ending the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Gas discharge and light emission due to ionization and excitation of low-pressure gas under high voltage. Minimum assumptions include a sealed glass tube with gas, a controllable high-voltage source, and a dark environment for visibility.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial dark state with voltage off and no emission; (2) causal action where a hand turns the voltage control upward; (3) onset of faint glow as gas begins to ionize; (4) intensification into a stable glow as voltage increases. Visibility constraints require a dark background and clear view of the tube and control to verify causal transitions.

manual: Experiment Title: Relationship between Earthquake Frequency and Building Height Amplitude (Resonance Demonstration)Subject: Physics – Natural ScienceExperiment Objective: To simulate how buildings of different heights respond differently to earthquake frequencies, understand resonance, and observe how vibration frequency affects oscillation amplitude.Experimental Equipment: Small horizontal vibration table with adjustable frequency, rigid base plate, three identical plastic balls, three slender flexible metal rods of different effective lengths (fixed vertically), fixing clamps or adhesive, power supply for vibration table.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Fix the base plate securely on the vibration table. Attach three identical plastic balls vertically to the base using slender flexible metal rods. Ensure rods are upright and balls are aligned in a row for easy comparison.2. Initial State: Set the vibration table to the lowest frequency. Turn on the table and confirm that the base vibrates horizontally with very small amplitude. Observe that all balls swing slightly.3. Frequency Increase: Gradually increase the vibration frequency in small steps. At each frequency, keep the vibration stable for a short time and observe the swing amplitude of each ball.4. Observation and Recording: Note that at certain frequencies, one ball swings much more strongly than the others, reaching a maximum amplitude, while the others remain relatively small.5. Completion: Continue increasing frequency until each ball has shown a maximum swing at least once. Turn off the vibration table and ensure all equipment is stable.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- At low frequencies, all balls show small, similar oscillations.- As frequency increases, one ball first shows a明显 increase in swing amplitude.- With further increase in frequency, the first ball’s amplitude decreases, while another ball reaches maximum amplitude.- Each ball has its own frequency at which the swing amplitude is greatest.Summary of Experimental Principle:This experiment demonstrates mechanical resonance. Each ball–rod system has a natural frequency determined mainly by the effective length and flexibility of the rod. When the vibration frequency of the base matches a ball’s natural frequency, resonance occurs, causing a sharp increase in oscillation amplitude. This models how buildings of different heights respond differently to earthquake frequencies: when earthquake frequency matches a building’s natural frequency, damage is most severe.

Weak Positive Correlation Plot: Using the same axis scale, input a second dataset where Y still increases with X but includes larger random variation. Generate a second scatter plot.5. Sequential Display: Present the strong positive correlation plot first, followed by the weak positive correlation plot for direct comparison.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Laser Beam Refracting at the Air–Water InterfaceI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Laser Beam Refraction at Air–Water InterfaceSubject: Physics – OpticsExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the refraction of light when a laser beam passes from air into water, and to explore how changing the angle of incidence affects the direction of the refracted beam.II. Experimental EquipmentClear rectangular water tank (glass or acrylic), clean water, low-power visible laser pointer, adjustable mount or hand-held support for the laser, darkened background or room, camera fixed on a tripod for side-view time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the clear tank with water to about three-quarters full and place it on a stable table. Darken the background to improve beam visibility. Fix the camera on a tripod to obtain a clear side view of the tank, ensuring the focus remains fixed throughout recording.2. Initial Alignment: Turn on the laser and position it in air so that the beam strikes the water surface at an oblique angle. Ensure the beam enters the water through the side wall or top surface and remains visible in both air and water.3. Core Operation: Slowly tilt the laser source to change the angle of incidence while keeping the laser position steady. Record the process continuously with the fixed-focus camera.4. Observation: Observe the path of the laser beam in air and its changed direction after entering the water. Repeat for several different angles of incidence.5. Completion: Turn off the laser, stop recording, and safely store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In air, the laser beam travels in a straight line.2. At the air–water interface, the beam changes direction.3. Inside the water, the refracted beam bends toward the normal compared with the incident beam in air.4. As the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction also changes correspondingly.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the refraction of light at the boundary between two media with different refractive indices. When light travels from air (lower refractive index) into water (higher refractive index), its speed decreases and its direction changes. The relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction follows Snell’s law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the refractive indices of air and water, respectively.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a low-power laser to ensure safety; never look directly into the laser beam. Keep the camera focus fixed to ensure consistent observation. Avoid shaking the tank during recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Tossed Dumbbell Rotating in Midair Following a Parabolic PathI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tossed Dumbbell Rotating in Midair Following a Parabolic Path2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics - Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To observe that the center of mass of a freely rotating rigid body follows a parabolic trajectory under gravity, while its rotation is independent of translational motion; to visually demonstrate projectile motion and rotational motion using time-lapse photography with fixed camera focus.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal dumbbell (small, symmetrical), open indoor or outdoor space, tripod-mounted camera or smartphone, fixed-focus setting enabled, stable background for reference, optional time-lapse or high-frame-rate recording mode.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Select an open space with minimal airflow. Mount the camera on a tripod, frame the entire expected motion region, and fix focus and exposure. Ensure the background is static for trajectory reference.Core Operation: Hold the metal dumbbell at chest height. Toss it smoothly into the air with a forward component, imparting visible rotation. Release cleanly so that the dumbbell is in free flight without further contact.Recording: Allow the camera to continuously record or capture time-lapse images during the entire flight until the dumbbell exits the frame or lands.Conclusion: Stop recording after the dumbbell completes its visible trajectory. Review the footage frame by frame if necessary.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The dumbbell leaves the hand and moves upward and forward.2. During flight, the dumbbell rotates steadily about its center.3. The overall path of the dumbbell’s center of mass forms a smooth parabola.4. Rotation continues uniformly while the translational motion slows upward, stops momentarily at the peak, and accelerates downward.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates classical mechanics principles. Under the influence of gravity alone, the center of mass of a rigid body in free flight follows projectile motion, resulting in a parabolic trajectory. The rotational motion of the dumbbell depends on the torque applied during release and is independent of gravity’s effect on the center of mass. Thus, translation and rotation are decoupled, illustrating the independence of linear and rotational motion in the absence of external torques.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ice Melting on Dark vs Light Surfaces (Albedo Effect)2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how surface color (albedo) affects heat absorption and melting rate of ice, and to understand the ecological significance of albedo in Earth’s energy balance.II. Experimental Equipment- Two identical ice blocks (same size, shape, and mass)- One dark matte surface (e.g., black cardboard or cloth)- One white surface (e.g., white cardboard or paper)- Heat lamp (single overhead lamp) or direct sunlight- Flat tray or table- Camera or smartphone with tripod- Timer or clock (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the dark matte surface and the white surface side by side on a flat table, ensuring equal distance from the heat source.2. Placement of Ice: Place one identical ice block at the center of each surface. Confirm that both ice blocks start at the same time and condition.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly facing the ice blocks. Fix focus, angle, and exposure. Set the camera for time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Heat Exposure: Turn on the single overhead heat lamp or ensure both ice blocks are equally exposed to direct sunlight.5. Observation Period: Allow the ice blocks to melt without disturbance. Record the entire process until clear differences are visible.6. Completion: Stop recording once one ice block has melted significantly more than the other. Turn off the lamp and clean the area.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice blocks appear identical in size and shape, with no visible melting.2. Early Stage: The ice block on the dark surface begins to melt faster, forming water around its base earlier than the one on the white surface.3. Later Stage: The ice on the dark surface becomes noticeably smaller, while the ice on the white surface remains relatively larger.4. Final State: A clear difference in melting rate is observed, with more meltwater and reduced ice volume on the dark surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the albedo effect. Dark surfaces have low albedo and absorb more incoming radiation, converting it into heat, which accelerates ice melting. White surfaces have high albedo and reflect more radiation, reducing heat absorption and slowing melting. In ecology and climate systems, this principle explains why ice and snow loss can accelerate warming through positive feedback mechanisms.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both ice blocks are identical to maintain fairness.2. Use only one heat source to avoid uneven heating.3. Do not move the camera or ice blocks during recording.4. Avoid touching the ice during the experiment to prevent external heat interference.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Albedo effect and its influence on heat absorption and ice melting. Minimum assumptions: identical ice blocks, equal heat exposure, contrasting surface reflectivity. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, side-by-side comparison, clear view of surface color and ice size changes.

Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand capillary action and unsaturated seepage in fine sand by visually demonstrating how water rises upward through pore spaces after the base of a sand column is submerged.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent vertical tube (glass or acrylic), fine dry sand, shallow tray or dish, clean water, stand or clamp to hold tube vertically, camera or smartphone fixed on tripod for side-view time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Ensure the transparent tube is clean and dry. Seal or support the bottom so sand does not escape. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates capillary action and unsaturated seepage in fine-grained soils. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Live-cell Fluorescence Imaging of Glucocorticoid Receptor Nuclear TranslocationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescently Tagged Glucocorticoid Receptor Translocation from Cytoplasm to Nucleus2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe in real time the hormone-induced nuclear translocation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) using live-cell fluorescence microscopy, and to understand receptor-mediated signal transduction.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentLive cultured mammalian cells expressing green fluorescent protein–tagged glucocorticoid receptor (GFP-GR); cell culture medium; glucocorticoid hormone solution (e.g., dexamethasone); two glass-bottom culture dishes; live-cell fluorescence microscope with temperature and CO₂ control; micropipette; computer with time-lapse imaging software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Plate equal numbers of GFP-GR–expressing cells into two identical culture dishes and incubate until cells adhere and spread. Place both dishes on the microscope stage side by side.2. Imaging Setup: Select the green fluorescence channel. Adjust exposure and focus on the cytoplasmic GFP signal. Fix the camera focus and imaging parameters for the entire experiment.3. Baseline Imaging: Begin time-lapse imaging and record baseline fluorescence in both dishes for a short period, confirming that GFP-GR is mainly cytoplasmic.4. Hormone Addition: During imaging, gently add glucocorticoid hormone to the left dish only, without disturbing focus or stage position. Do not add hormone to the right dish (control).5. Time-lapse Observation: Continue imaging for several minutes, capturing frames at regular intervals to record dynamic changes.6. Completion: Stop imaging after a clear difference between the two dishes is observed. Save and label the image sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In both dishes, green fluorescent GR is predominantly distributed in the cytoplasm, with weak nuclear signal.2. After Hormone Addition: In the left dish, fluorescence gradually decreases in the cytoplasm and accumulates in the nucleus, producing bright nuclear fluorescence.3. Control Dish: In the right dish, fluorescence distribution remains largely unchanged, staying cytoplasmic throughout imaging.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGlucocorticoid receptors are intracellular receptors that reside in the cytoplasm when inactive. Upon binding glucocorticoid hormone, the receptor undergoes a conformational change, dissociates from chaperone proteins, and translocates into the nucleus. The untreated dish serves as a control to demonstrate that the observed nuclear accumulation is specifically induced by hormone addition.

Experiment Title: Demonstrating the Relationship Between Frequency and Pitch Using an Oscilloscope2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how sound frequency determines pitch by observing waveform changes on an oscilloscope while keeping amplitude constant.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the oscilloscope and signal generator. Set the oscilloscope to time-domain display and adjust the time base to clearly show a low-frequency waveform.2. Frequency Adjustment: While keeping the amplitude constant, gradually increase the sound frequency in small steps (e.g., 100 Hz to 200 Hz to 400 Hz).5. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Smoke Streaklines over an Airfoil in a Wind TunnelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Smoke Streaklines over an Airfoil2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering (Aerodynamics)3. Experiment Objective: To visualize airflow patterns around a thin airfoil at different angles of attack using smoke streaklines, understand lift generation and flow separation, and master basic wind tunnel flow visualization methods.II. Experimental EquipmentLow-speed wind tunnel with transparent test section; thin airfoil model with rotation mount; smoke generator or smoke wire system; steady airflow control system; fixed-focus camera for time-lapse photography; angle-of-attack adjustment mechanism; lighting system.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Install the thin airfoil horizontally in the wind tunnel test section. Ensure the camera is fixed, focused, and aligned perpendicular to the test section. Turn on lighting for clear visualization.2. Flow Initialization: Start the wind tunnel and adjust to a steady, uniform airflow. Activate the smoke generator to produce continuous, parallel smoke lines upstream of the airfoil.3. Baseline Observation: Observe and record smoke streaklines at zero or small angle of attack, ensuring flow is steady and attached.4. Core Operation: Gradually rotate the airfoil to increase the angle of attack in small increments while maintaining constant airflow. Keep the camera fixed and record continuously (time-lapse).5. Termination: After reaching a high angle of attack and observing flow separation, return the airfoil to neutral, stop smoke generation, and shut down the wind tunnel.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Low Angle of Attack: Smoke streaklines remain smooth and attached to the airfoil surfaces, with slight acceleration over the upper surface.2. Moderate Angle of Attack: Upper-surface streaklines curve more strongly, indicating increased lift; wake behind the airfoil thickens.3. High Angle of Attack: Smoke streaklines separate from the upper surface, showing flow separation and a turbulent wake (stall behavior).V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates fundamental aerodynamic principles. According to fluid dynamics and Bernoulli’s principle, increased airflow velocity over the upper surface leads to lower pressure and lift. As angle of attack increases, adverse pressure gradients grow, eventually causing boundary layer separation. Smoke streaklines act as flow tracers, making these flow features directly visible.VI. Experimental PrecautionsMaintain steady airflow; adjust angle of attack slowly; ensure smoke density is uniform; keep camera fixed to preserve time-lapse comparability.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Bench-top Enzyme Assay Demonstrating Phosphate Release via Molybdate Blue Color FormationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Enzymatic Phosphate Release Using a Molybdate-Based Colorimetric Assay2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate enzymatic hydrolysis of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by comparing an active enzyme with a heat-denatured control, and to visualize released inorganic phosphate through blue color formation using a molybdate-based detection reagent.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents- Clear microcentrifuge tubes or small test tubes (2)- Tube rack- Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate solution (substrate)- Enzyme solution (e.g., phosphatase or aldolase/phosphatase system)- Heat-denatured enzyme (boiled, inactive control)- Molybdate-based phosphate detection reagent (e.g., ammonium molybdate with reducing agent)- Micropipettes and tips- Timer- Camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear tubes in a rack. Label the left tube Active Enzyme and the right tube Denatured Enzyme. Add equal volumes of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate solution to each tube.2. Enzyme Addition: Add active enzyme to the left tube and heat-denatured enzyme to the right tube. Mix gently without creating bubbles.3. Incubation: Incubate both tubes briefly at room temperature (or specified assay temperature) to allow enzymatic reaction.4. Detection Reaction: Add an equal volume of molybdate-based phosphate detection reagent to each tube. Mix gently.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and record the tubes using time-lapse photography to capture color development.6. Completion: After observation, dispose of reagents according to laboratory safety guidelines and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes are clear and colorless before addition of detection reagent.2. After Incubation and Reagent Addition: The tube with active enzyme gradually develops a blue color, indicating phosphate release.3. Control Result: The tube with heat-denatured enzyme shows little to no blue color change, remaining nearly colorless or faintly tinted.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on enzymatic hydrolysis of phosphate-containing substrates. Active enzyme catalyzes the release of inorganic phosphate from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. The released phosphate reacts with molybdate under acidic conditions to form a phosphomolybdate complex, which is reduced to produce a blue-colored compound. Heat-denatured enzyme lacks catalytic activity and therefore releases little or no phosphate, serving as a negative control.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Triangle Symmetry Transformation About the x-axis VisualizationSubject: Mathematics – Geometry (Plane Coordinate Geometry)Objective: To visually demonstrate the symmetry transformation of a triangle about the x-axis, understand coordinate changes under reflection, and identify corresponding vertices.II. Connect them with solid black lines to form triangle ABC. Label each vertex with its coordinates.3. Symmetry Axis: Highlight the x-axis (y=0) using a red dashed line to indicate the axis of symmetry.4. Symmetric Figure: Reflect each vertex of triangle ABC across the x-axis to obtain A′(1,-2), B′(3,-2), and C′(2,-1). Draw triangle A′B′C′ using solid blue lines and label the coordinates.5. Correspondence: Draw green dashed lines connecting A to A′, B to B′, and C to C′, showing perpendicular correspondence to the x-axis.6. Experimental Principle SummaryReflection about the x-axis is a geometric transformation where the x-coordinate of each point remains unchanged, and the y-coordinate changes sign.
