manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Capillary Rise of Water Compared to Oil in a Paper TowelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Capillary Rise of Water Compared to Oil in a Paper Towel2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the capillary rise behavior of water and cooking oil in identical paper towel strips, and to understand the role of polarity, intermolecular forces, and adhesion in liquid transport through porous materials.II. Experimental MaterialsPaper towel (same brand and thickness), scissors, two transparent containers, blue-colored water, yellow cooking oil, ruler or marker, flat surface, camera or smartphone with tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut two identical paper towel strips of equal length and width. Place two transparent containers side by side on a flat surface.2. Liquid Setup: Pour blue-colored water into the left container and yellow cooking oil into the right container, ensuring similar liquid levels.3. Placement: Simultaneously dip one end of each paper towel strip into the corresponding liquid. Ensure both strips start at the same height and orientation.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position so both paper towels are fully visible. Start time-lapse or accelerated recording.5. Observation Period: Allow liquids to rise along the paper towels for a short period (accelerated for demonstration).6. Completion: Stop recording once a clear difference in liquid rise is visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both paper towels are dry above the liquid surface.2. During the Experiment: Blue water rises quickly and higher along the paper towel fibers. Yellow oil rises more slowly and to a lower height.3. Final State: A clear height difference is observed, with water having a greater capillary rise than oil.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePaper towels contain many tiny pores that act as capillaries. Water molecules are polar and form strong hydrogen bonds with cellulose fibers, resulting in strong adhesion and capillary action. Cooking oil is nonpolar, has weaker adhesion to cellulose, and higher viscosity, so it rises more slowly and to a lesser extent. The experiment demonstrates how molecular properties influence liquid transport in porous biological materials.VI. Experimental Notes1. Ensure paper towel strips are identical to ensure fair comparison.2. Do not move the containers during recording to maintain spatial consistency.3. Use accelerated recording to fit the observation into a short demonstration video.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring System Oscillating After Being Stretched and ReleasedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mass–Spring System Oscillation After Vertical Stretching2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering (Dynamics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the oscillatory motion of a mass–spring system after being stretched and released from rest, verify simple harmonic motion characteristics, and provide a clear visual record using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentCeiling-mounted helical spring (elastic, visible coils), mass/weight with hook, rigid ceiling support, ruler or scale (optional, for reference), camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse or fixed-position recording function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup Preparation: Securely fix the spring to the ceiling support. Attach the mass to the lower end of the spring and allow it to hang vertically at rest. Place the camera on a tripod facing the system from the side; fix focus and framing so the entire motion range is visible.2. Initial State Adjustment: Ensure the mass is stationary at its natural equilibrium position. Confirm the camera focus is locked and recording or time-lapse mode is ready.3. Stretching Operation: Using one hand, pull the mass straight downward along the vertical line of the spring. Stretch it smoothly to a visible displacement without sideways motion.4. Release: Hold briefly to ensure the mass is at rest, then release the mass suddenly without applying additional force.5. Recording and Completion: Allow the mass to oscillate freely for several cycles while recording. Stop recording after the oscillation amplitude visibly decreases.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mass hangs motionless at equilibrium, spring slightly stretched by gravity.2. After Release: The mass moves upward, passes the equilibrium position, then moves downward, repeating vertical oscillations.3. During Motion: The oscillation is periodic; the mass slows near the highest and lowest points and moves fastest near equilibrium. Over time, the amplitude gradually decreases due to damping.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates a classic mass–spring system undergoing simple harmonic motion. When displaced from equilibrium and released, the restoring force of the spring (described by Hooke’s law, F = −kx) causes the mass to oscillate. Gravity shifts the equilibrium position but does not change the oscillation form. Energy alternates between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy, with gradual energy loss due to air resistance and internal friction, leading to damping.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Rotating a Wire Loop Between Magnet PolesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating a Wire Loop Between Magnet Poles (Electromagnetic Induction)2. Subject: Physics – Electricity and Magnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe electromagnetic induction by rotating a rectangular wire loop between the north and south poles of a fixed horseshoe magnet, and to understand how changing magnetic flux induces electric current.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular wire loop with axle, horseshoe magnet with marked N and S poles, connecting wires, analog galvanometer, support stand, hand crank or motor (for steady rotation), camera fixed on tripod (focus locked for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the horseshoe magnet on the stand so that the north and south poles face each other, leaving a gap between them. Circuit Connection: Connect the two ends of the wire loop to the analog galvanometer using connecting wires, ensuring good electrical contact.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the loop and galvanometer. Fix focus and keep the viewpoint unchanged.4. Core Operation: Rotate the wire loop steadily using a hand crank or motor, keeping the speed approximately constant.5. Observation: Observe the galvanometer needle while the loop rotates continuously.6. Completion: Stop rotation, disconnect the circuit, and power off recording equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the loop is stationary, the galvanometer needle stays at zero.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen the rectangular wire loop rotates in the magnetic field between the north and south poles, the magnetic flux through the loop changes continuously. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Bulb Brightness Using Copper Wire and Iron Wire2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Electricity)3. Experiment Objective: To verify that, under identical conditions, a bulb connected with a copper wire of fixed length is brighter than when connected with an iron wire of the same length, and to understand the effect of conductor resistance on current.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (1, appropriate voltage), small bulb with holder (1), switch (1), copper wire (1 piece, fixed length), iron wire (1 piece, same length as copper wire), connecting wires, insulating base.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the battery, switch, and bulb on an insulating surface. Ensure the bulb is intact and all wires are clean and dry.2. Circuit Setup with Copper Wire:   (1) Connect the positive terminal of the battery to the switch.   (2) Connect the switch to the bulb holder.   (3) Insert the copper wire of fixed length between the bulb holder and the negative terminal of the battery to complete the circuit.   (4) Check that all connections are firm and the wiring order is correct.3. Observation 1: Close the switch and observe the brightness of the bulb. Keep the switch closed for a short, fixed time.4. Circuit Setup with Iron Wire:   (1) Open the switch to disconnect the circuit.   (2) Remove the copper wire without changing any other components.   (3) Replace it with the iron wire of the same length in the same position.   (4) Ensure the wiring order and all other conditions remain unchanged.5. Observation 2: Close the switch again and observe the brightness of the bulb.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the copper wire is connected and the switch is closed, the bulb lights up brightly.2. When the iron wire of the same length is used under identical conditions, the bulb also lights up, but its brightness is noticeably weaker than with the copper wire.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDifferent metal wires have different electrical resistances. Copper has a lower resistivity than iron. Under the same voltage and wire length, the copper wire has smaller resistance, allowing a larger current to flow through the circuit, so the bulb appears brighter. The iron wire has higher resistance, resulting in a smaller current and a dimmer bulb.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Voiced vs Voiceless Plosive Sounds Shown by Candle Flame MovementI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Voiced and Voiceless Plosive Sounds Using Candle Flame Movement2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the difference between voiced and voiceless plosive sounds by observing candle flame movement caused by airflow during speech, and to help learners understand the articulatory and aerodynamic differences between these two types of plosives.II. Experimental Equipment1. A stable table and chair2. One small candle and a lighter or matches3. Camera or smartphone (capable of video or time-lapse recording)4. Tripod or fixed stand for the camera5. Quiet indoor environment with minimal air disturbanceIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Place the candle upright on the table and light it.   - Seat the speaker comfortably at the table.   - Adjust the distance so that the candle flame is approximately 3–5 cm from the speaker’s mouth.   - Set the camera on a tripod directly facing the speaker’s mouth and the candle, and fix the focus to avoid refocusing during recording.2. Recording Setup:   - Ensure the room is still, with no wind or fans.   - Start video or time-lapse recording, keeping both the speaker’s mouth and the candle flame clearly in frame.3. Core Operation:   - The speaker first produces voiceless plosive syllables (such as /pa/, /ta/, /ka/) toward the candle, one at a time, with short pauses between repetitions.   - Next, the speaker produces voiced plosive syllables (such as /ba/, /da/, /ga/) toward the candle, maintaining a similar speaking volume and distance.   - Alternate between voiceless and voiced plosives if time allows, keeping articulation clear and controlled.4. Completion:   - Stop recording after all target syllables have been produced.   - Extinguish the candle safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. During voiceless plosive production:   - The candle flame shows a clear, sudden, and relatively strong flicker or deflection due to a burst of air released from the mouth.2. During voiced plosive production:   - The candle flame shows weaker movement, smaller flickers, or remains comparatively steadier, as airflow is reduced by vocal fold vibration.3. Comparative Observation:   - The difference in flame movement between voiceless and voiced plosives is visually noticeable when syllables are produced under similar conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVoiceless plosive sounds are produced without vocal fold vibration, allowing higher oral air pressure to build up and be released suddenly, creating a strong airflow that visibly disturbs the candle flame. Voiced plosive sounds involve vocal fold vibration, which reduces the airflow released at the mouth, resulting in weaker flame movement. The candle flame thus serves as a visual indicator of aerodynamic differences between voiced and voiceless plosives.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Maintain a constant distance between mouth and candle throughout the experiment.2. Avoid exaggerated blowing; articulate speech sounds naturally.3. Ensure fire safety at all times and extinguish the candle immediately after the experiment.4. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure clear observation of flame movement.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The visual differentiation of voiced and voiceless plosive sounds based on airflow strength during speech. Minimum assumptions: a stable candle flame reacts visibly to airflow, and voiced and voiceless plosives differ in aerodynamic output. Expected phased storyline: (1) stable candle flame at rest; (2) production of voiceless plosives causing strong, sudden flame deflection; (3) production of voiced plosives causing weaker or minimal flame movement; (4) clear visual contrast between the two conditions. Visibility constraints: the candle flame and speaker’s mouth must remain in frame, with fixed focus and minimal background air disturbance for reliable comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Swelling and Bursting of Red Blood Cells in Distilled WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Swelling and Bursting of Red Blood Cells in Distilled Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Ecology & Evolutionary Biology (Cell Biology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe, under a light microscope, the osmotic response of red blood cells when exposed to distilled water, and to understand the principle of osmosis across the cell membrane. Students will learn to focus a microscope, add liquid at the edge of a coverslip, and record dynamic cellular changes using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsLight microscope with camera interface, microscope slide with a prepared red blood cell smear (in isotonic saline), coverslip, dropper or micropipette, distilled water, absorbent paper or tissue, camera or computer software for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation and Focusing: Place the prepared red blood cell slide on the microscope stage. Turn on the light source and start with low magnification, then switch to high magnification. Carefully adjust the coarse and fine focus until individual red blood cells are clearly visible as small, round, biconcave discs.2. Camera Setup: Fix the microscope camera or recording device in position. Lock the focus so that it will not change during recording. Begin continuous observation or start time-lapse recording.3. Addition of Distilled Water: Using a dropper, gently place one drop of distilled water at the edge of the coverslip. At the opposite edge, use absorbent paper to help draw the distilled water under the coverslip by capillary action.4. Observation and Recording: Keep the microscope focus unchanged. Observe and record the gradual diffusion of distilled water into the field of view and the resulting changes in red blood cells over time.5. Completion: After the main phenomena are clearly observed, stop recording. Turn off the microscope light and clean the workspace according to laboratory rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Red blood cells appear normal, with clear outlines and a biconcave disc shape.2. Early Stage after Adding Distilled Water: As distilled water diffuses in, red blood cells begin to swell and become more spherical.3. Later Stage: The swollen red blood cells lose their distinct shape, and some cells burst (hemolysis), causing the cells to fade or disappear, leaving a lighter background in the field of view.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates osmosis across the semi-permeable membrane of red blood cells. Distilled water is hypotonic relative to the cytoplasm of red blood cells. When exposed to distilled water, water molecules move into the cells by osmosis, causing them to swell. Because red blood cells lack a rigid cell wall, excessive water intake leads to membrane rupture, a process known as hemolysis. The observed swelling and bursting directly reflect the osmotic imbalance between the intracellular and extracellular environments.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add distilled water gently to avoid shifting the coverslip or washing cells out of view.2. Do not refocus the microscope during observation, as this affects time-lapse consistency.3. Handle biological slides carefully and follow biosafety and disposal regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Osmosis in animal cells, demonstrated by red blood cell swelling and hemolysis in hypotonic distilled water. Minimum assumptions: red blood cells have a semi-permeable membrane, distilled water is hypotonic, and the microscope remains fixed in focus.Phased storyline: Phase 1 – Stable baseline: clearly focused, normal biconcave red blood cells. Phase 2 – Intervention: distilled water enters under the coverslip by diffusion without disturbing focus. Phase 3 – Response: red blood cells gradually swell and become spherical. Phase 4 – Outcome: membranes rupture and cells fade or disappear. Visibility constraints: field of view must remain stable, focus unchanged, and changes must be observable within a shortened time window suitable for a 10–15 second demonstration.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Impulse Response of a Mass–Spring–Damper SystemSubject: Engineering – Mechanical EngineeringObjective: To observe the free vibration and damping characteristics of a mass–spring–damper system after a brief external impulse, and to understand the dynamic response governed by second-order system theory.II. Experimental EquipmentBench-mounted mass–spring–damper assembly (vertical orientation), rubber mallet, stable workbench, camera (fixed focus, time-lapse or continuous recording mode).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the mass–spring–damper system to the bench so it hangs freely without obstruction. Ensure the mass is at rest at its static equilibrium position.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the system. Fix focus and framing so the entire motion range of the mass is visible. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.3. Core Operation: Using one hand, apply a single brief strike to the mass with a rubber mallet. The strike should be quick and impulsive, not sustained.4. Withdrawal: Immediately withdraw the hand and mallet, leaving the system completely untouched.5. Observation Period: Allow the mass to oscillate freely until the motion visibly decays toward rest.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mass is stationary at equilibrium.2. Immediately after Strike: The mass is suddenly displaced and begins oscillating.3. Free Vibration: The mass undergoes oscillatory motion about the equilibrium position.4. Damping Effect: The amplitude of oscillation decreases gradually with time until the mass comes to rest.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe system behaves as a second-order mass–spring–damper system. A brief mallet strike provides an impulse input, imparting initial velocity to the mass. After the impulse is removed, the system undergoes free vibration governed by Newton’s second law. The spring provides a restoring force proportional to displacement, while the damper provides a resistive force proportional to velocity. Energy is dissipated by damping, causing the oscillation amplitude to decay over time.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: impulse response of a linear mass–spring–damper system under free vibration with damping. Experimental Equipment and Materials- Two identical clear glass beakers (250 mL)- Clean water (approximately 100 mL per beaker)- Cooking oil (approximately 10 mL per beaker)- Bile-salt substitute (e.g., dishwashing liquid or food-grade emulsifier)- Dropper or pipette- Stopwatch or timer- Camera mounted on tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a lab bench. Pour equal volumes of water into each beaker, followed by equal volumes of cooking oil. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: DAC Feeding RC Filter Driving LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: DAC Feeding RC Filter Driving LED with Gradual Rise/Fall2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a microcontroller DAC output, when passed through an RC low-pass filter, produces a smooth analog voltage that drives an LED to show gradual brightness rise and fall; to understand DAC operation, RC filtering, and time constant effects.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrocontroller with DAC output (e.g., STM32/ESP32), USB power cable, resistor (e.g., 1–10 kΩ), capacitor (e.g., 10–100 µF), LED, current-limiting resistor (e.g., 220–330 Ω), breadboard, jumper wires, fixed-focus camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microcontroller and breadboard on the workbench. Fix the camera position and focus to cover the entire circuit area.2. Circuit Assembly: Connect the DAC output pin to the resistor, then to the capacitor to ground, forming an RC low-pass filter. Connect the filtered output to the LED through a current-limiting resistor, with the LED cathode to ground.3. Programming: Upload a program that continuously updates the DAC value in a ramp-up and ramp-down pattern (e.g., incrementing and decrementing digital values in a loop).4. Operation: Power the microcontroller via USB. Start the time-lapse recording. Allow the program to run continuously without adjusting the camera or circuit.5. Completion: After observing several cycles of LED brightness change, stop recording and power off the system.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: LED is off or dim at startup.2. During Operation: As the DAC value increases, the LED brightness increases gradually rather than abruptly.3. Falling Phase: When the DAC value decreases, the LED brightness fades smoothly.4. Repetition: The rise and fall repeat continuously, suitable for time-lapse capture.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe DAC converts digital values from the microcontroller into a stepped analog voltage. The RC low-pass filter smooths these steps due to its time constant (τ = RC), attenuating high-frequency components and producing a gradual voltage change. The LED responds to this smoothed voltage/current, resulting in a visible gradual rise and fall in brightness rather than sudden changes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct polarity of LED and capacitor; include a current-limiting resistor to prevent LED damage; keep camera focus fixed; avoid touching the circuit during recording.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the specific binding between antigens and antibodies using antigen-coated latex beads, and to visually observe agglutination as evidence of antigen–antibody recognition.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Two petri dishes placed on a clean lab bench2. Antigen-coated latex bead suspension (equal volume in each dish)3. Antibody solution specific to the antigen (test sample)4. Control solution without specific antibody (e.g., buffer or non-specific serum)5. Red-capped dropper (for antibody solution)6. Blue-capped dropper (for control solution)7. Disposable gloves8. Camera fixed above the lab bench for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear disposable gloves. Place two petri dishes side by side on the lab bench. Add equal volumes of antigen-coated latex bead suspension into each dish. Ensure the beads are evenly dispersed and appear uniformly milky.2. Addition of Reagents: Using the red-capped dropper, add a few drops of the antibody solution into the left petri dish. Using the blue-capped dropper, add an equal number of drops of the control solution into the right petri dish.3. Mixing: Gently rock both petri dishes by hand in a circular motion to ensure thorough mixing, avoiding splashing or spillage.4. Recording: Keep the camera focus fixed and stable. Record the reaction using time-lapse photography while the dishes remain on the bench.5. Completion: After clear phenomena are observed, stop rocking the dishes and end the recording. Dispose of biological materials according to laboratory safety rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In both petri dishes, latex beads are evenly suspended, forming a uniform, cloudy appearance with no visible clumps.2. Experimental Dish (Left): After addition of the antibody solution and gentle rocking, visible clumping of latex beads gradually appears. Beads aggregate into larger clusters, and the suspension becomes uneven and grainy.3. Control Dish (Right): After addition of the control solution and rocking, the latex beads remain evenly dispersed with no obvious aggregation or clumping.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLatex bead agglutination is based on the specific binding between antigens and antibodies. The latex beads are coated with a known antigen. When a solution containing the corresponding specific antibody is added, each antibody can bind to antigens on different beads, cross-linking them into visible aggregates. This agglutination can be directly observed by the naked eye. In the absence of specific antibodies, no cross-linking occurs, and the beads remain evenly suspended. This experiment demonstrates the specificity and biological recognition principle of antigen–antibody interactions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use equal volumes of latex bead suspension and reagents for valid comparison.2. Avoid vigorous shaking, which may cause bubbles or non-specific aggregation.3. Ensure droppers are not cross-contaminated between solutions.4. Maintain a fixed camera position to ensure accurate time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: antigen–antibody specific binding leading to visible latex bead agglutination. Minimum assumptions: latex beads are pre-coated with antigen; antibody solution is specific; control lacks specificity. Phased storyline: (1) static setup with two identical bead suspensions; (2) differential addition of antibody vs control using color-coded droppers; (3) gentle rocking as the causal trigger; (4) emergence of bead clumping only in the antibody-treated dish while the control remains uniform. Visibility constraints: overhead or slightly angled fixed camera, clear view of bead texture changes, and synchronized observation of both dishes for comparison.

Equipment and MaterialsGranulated sugar (200 g), saucepan or heat-resistant beaker, hot plate, thermometer (optional), two shallow trays, metal slab, ice pack or ice bath, heat-resistant gloves, spatula, camera with tripod.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Soap Film Illuminated by White Light Showing Shifting Color BandsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Soap Film Interference ColorsSubject: Physics – Optics (Natural Science)Objective: To observe thin-film interference by creating a vertical soap film on a rectangular wire frame, illuminating it with steady white light, and analyzing color changes as the film drains and is gently tilted.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular wire frame with handle, soap solution (water with detergent and a small amount of glycerin), shallow tray, steady white light source (lamp), dark or neutral background.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour soap solution into the tray. Ensure the light source is steady and positioned to illuminate the frame uniformly. Place a dark background behind the setup.2. Film Formation: Dip the rectangular wire frame fully into the soap solution and slowly lift it out, forming a uniform soap film across the frame.3. Vertical Setup: Hold the frame vertically so gravity causes the film to drain downward.4. Illumination: Shine steady white light onto the film at a fixed angle. Avoid flickering or changing light intensity.5. Observation and Tilt: Observe the film as it slowly drains. Gently tilt the frame slightly left or right to alter thickness distribution while continuing observation.6. Completion: After observation, allow the film to break naturally, then clean and store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the soap film appears mostly transparent. As time passes, horizontal and curved colored bands appear and shift downward. The colors change continuously as the film becomes thinner. Gentle tilting causes the color bands to redistribute and move, reflecting changes in local thickness.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe observed colors arise from thin-film interference. White light reflects from the front and back surfaces of the soap film. Due to varying film thickness caused by gravity-driven drainage and tilting, different wavelengths undergo constructive or destructive interference at different positions, producing shifting color bands.VI. PrecautionsAvoid air currents, keep lighting steady, and handle the frame gently to prevent premature film rupture.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: thin-film interference in a draining soap film under white light. Minimum assumptions: a continuous soap film with varying thickness, steady illumination, and gravity-driven drainage. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Live-cell GFP fluorescence with excitation light on/offSubject: Engineering – Biomedical EngineeringObjective: To observe green fluorescence from live cells expressing GFP under blue excitation light, and compare it with transmitted-light images of the same field by switching excitation on and off.II. Equipment and MaterialsInverted fluorescence microscope with blue excitation and GFP emission filter set; transmitted-light (brightfield) illumination; live cells expressing GFP cultured on a glass-bottom dish; stage-top incubator (optional); computer with imaging software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on microscope, light source, and camera. Place the live GFP-expressing cell dish on the microscope stage and focus under transmitted light.2. Transmitted-Light Imaging: Adjust focus and illumination to obtain a clear brightfield image of cell morphology. Record the image.3. Fluorescence Imaging (Excitation ON): Switch on blue excitation light and insert the GFP filter set. Observe and record green fluorescence from the same field.4. Excitation OFF: Turn off blue excitation light. Observe that green fluorescence disappears while cells remain visible in transmitted light.5. Alternating Observation: Repeatedly switch between transmitted-light mode and blue-excitation fluorescence mode to confirm reversible fluorescence behavior in the same cells.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Under transmitted light, cells appear transparent with visible outlines and internal structures.Excitation ON: When blue excitation light is applied, cells emit bright green fluorescence localized within the cytoplasm.Excitation OFF: When excitation is turned off, green fluorescence disappears immediately, and only transmitted-light cell morphology remains.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGFP is a fluorescent protein that absorbs blue light and emits green light. In live cells expressing GFP, fluorescence occurs only when the appropriate excitation light is applied. Transmitted-light imaging provides non-fluorescent morphological reference of the same field.VI. PrecautionsMinimize exposure time to reduce photobleaching and phototoxicity; maintain cells in physiological conditions; ensure the same field of view is used for all imaging modes.

Core Operation (Blending): Apply the brush to the shaded area using light, even pressure. Move in small, controlled circular or linear motions to redistribute graphite evenly.4. Boundary Control: Gradually approach the edge of the shaded region, slowing down and stopping the brush before touching adjacent unblended areas.5. Experimental Principle SummaryThe blending technique relies on mechanical redistribution of graphite particles across the paper surface using a paper brush. Even pressure ensures consistent spread of graphite, reducing visible hatching. Stopping before unblended areas and lifting the brush cleanly preserves clear boundaries, creating contrast between blended and unblended regions.VI. Experiment Title: Catalase Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide with Inhibitor Comparison2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Biochemistry/Enzymology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe catalase-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and demonstrate how an inhibitor reduces enzyme activity through visual comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTwo transparent test tubes (same size); one tinted test tube or sleeve; test tube rack; catalase solution (e.g., yeast or liver extract); hydrogen peroxide solution (3%); enzyme inhibitor (e.g., copper sulfate solution or heat-denatured catalase); droppers or pipettes; stopwatch or timer; fixed camera on tripod for time-lapse recording; safety goggles and gloves.III. Material Addition: Add an equal mass of crystalline sugar into the left beaker. Add an equal mass of sugar glass shards into the right beaker.3. Stirring: Gently stir both beakers simultaneously and equally using separate glass rods.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and record the dissolution process using time-lapse photography.5. Completion: Stop stirring once clear differences in dissolution behavior are observed.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, both sugars are visible as solid particles. During stirring, sugar glass in the right beaker rapidly disperses and dissolves, causing quick clarification. Crystalline sugar in the left beaker dissolves more slowly, with visible granules persisting for a longer time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSugar glass is an amorphous solid with higher free energy and greater molecular mobility, allowing water to penetrate and dissolve it rapidly. This demonstrates the influence of solid-state structure on dissolution rate, an important concept in pharmacy.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Chocolate Softening and Liquefying Under Gentle HeatingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Chocolate Softening and Liquefying Under Gentle Heating2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering (Heat Transfer and Phase Change)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how gentle and continuous heat input causes a solid chocolate piece to soften and eventually liquefy, and to relate this process to heat transfer and phase change principles.II. Experimental Equipment1. Metal pan or metal plate (clean, flat surface)2. Single piece of solid chocolate (uniform size, unwrapped)3. Heating source (electric hot plate or induction cooker with low-power setting)4. Heat-resistant surface or support5. Camera or recording device (for continuous recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal pan on the heating source. Ensure the heating setting is adjusted to a low, gentle, and steady level. Confirm the chocolate is at room temperature and solid.2. Placement: Place one single piece of chocolate at the center of the metal pan. Start continuous video recording before heating begins.3. Heating: Turn on the heating source and maintain steady, gentle heating. Do not stir, press, or move the chocolate during the experiment.4. Continuous Observation: Keep the camera fixed and record continuously for several minutes while the chocolate is heated.5. Completion: Once the chocolate has visibly softened and largely liquefied, turn off the heat and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chocolate maintains a solid shape with clear edges and matte surface.2. Early Heating Stage: The surface of the chocolate becomes slightly glossy; edges begin to round as softening starts.3. Softening Stage: The chocolate gradually loses its rigid shape, slumps outward, and spreads slightly on the metal surface.4. Liquefaction Stage: The chocolate becomes semi-liquid to liquid, forming a smooth, glossy melted pool while remaining stationary on the pan.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates heat transfer and phase change. Heat is transferred from the heated metal pan to the chocolate mainly through conduction. As the chocolate absorbs thermal energy, its temperature increases until it reaches its melting range. At this point, the solid chocolate undergoes a phase change, softening and then liquefying. Continuous gentle heating ensures a gradual and observable transition, illustrating the relationship between energy input, material properties, and state change.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use gentle heating to avoid burning or rapid boiling of chocolate.2. Do not touch the pan during heating to prevent burns.3. Keep the camera stable to ensure clear observation of gradual changes.4. Ensure only one piece of chocolate is used to maintain experimental clarity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Gentle heat transfer causing phase change in chocolate. Minimum assumptions: chocolate starts solid at room temperature; metal pan conducts heat steadily; no external disturbance. Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – solid chocolate rests on pan; Phase 2 – heat conduction raises temperature, surface gloss appears; Phase 3 – structural softening and spreading; Phase 4 – visible liquefaction into a melted pool. Key causal transition is steady heat input leading to melting. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear view of chocolate shape, surface texture, and gradual change over time.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Visualization of Acoustic Performance Comparison of Architectural MaterialsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Acoustic Differences Between Sound-Absorbing and Reflective Materials2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: Using sound wave ripples (wave graphics) to visually represent sound propagation, compare and understand the acoustic performance differences between sound-absorbing materials (sponge) and reflective materials (glass), and enhance intuitive understanding of architectural acoustic design principles.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Sound source: Small speaker or simulated point sound source (icon or graphic)2. Materials under test: Sponge panel (sound-absorbing material), glass panel (sound-reflective material)3. Visualization medium: Wave ripple graphics or animation representing sound waves4. Experimental platform: Physical tabletop demonstration or digital/animation-based visualization interfaceIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the sponge panel and glass panel separately in front of the sound source at equal distances. Ensure the surrounding environment is visually neutral to clearly observe wave propagation.2. Baseline Emission: Activate the sound source. Display circular sound wave ripples propagating outward uniformly in free space to represent initial sound emission.3. Sponge Material Test: Direct the sound waves toward the sponge panel. Observe and record changes in wave ripples as they contact the sponge surface.4. Glass Material Test: Reset the visualization. Direct the sound waves toward the glass panel. Observe and record changes in wave ripples as they contact the glass surface.5. Comparison Observation: Place sponge and glass panels side by side (optional accelerated step) and emit sound waves simultaneously to visually compare wave behavior.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sound waves propagate outward from the source as evenly spaced circular ripples.2. Sponge Interaction: When waves reach the sponge, the ripples weaken, fade, or reduce in amplitude, with minimal reflection visible.3. Glass Interaction: When waves reach the glass, the ripples are strongly reflected, showing clear rebound waves traveling back into the space.4. Comparative Result: The sponge side shows diminished wave intensity, while the glass side shows strong, clear reflected ripples.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on architectural acoustics principles. Sound-absorbing materials like sponge have porous structures that convert sound energy into heat through friction, reducing reflected sound. Reflective materials like glass have smooth, rigid surfaces that reflect most incident sound waves. Visualizing sound as wave ripples allows intuitive comparison of absorption versus reflection, supporting acoustic material selection in architectural design.VI. Experimental Notes1. Wave graphics are symbolic representations and focus on relative differences rather than precise physical measurements.2. Ensure identical sound source strength and distance for fair comparison.3. For short demonstrations, wave propagation speed and fading may be visually accelerated.

Experiment Title: PIR Motion Sensor Automatically Turning on a Lamp2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To understand the working principle of a Passive Infrared (PIR) motion sensor and verify that it can automatically control a lamp based on human movement. Core Operation:   - A person opens the door and enters the room, passing through the PIR sensor’s detection zone.   - The person pauses briefly after entering, then stands still without moving.   - After a short delay, the person turns around and leaves the room, exiting through the door.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt-Induced Colloid Clumping in MilkI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ionic Interaction Screening: Salt-Induced Colloid Clumping in Milk2. Subject: Biology – Natural Science (Colloids and Ionic Interactions)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how adding salt affects the stability of milk as a colloidal system, and to understand how ionic interaction screening leads to protein aggregation.II. Experimental MaterialsTransparent glass cups (2 identical glasses), fresh milk (sufficient to fill each glass equally), table salt (sodium chloride), spoon (1), stable table surface, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent glasses side by side on a stable table. Pour equal volumes of milk into each glass. Ensure both glasses are clearly visible within the camera frame.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both glasses remain in view. Enable time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Control Setup: Leave the left glass untouched as the control group.4. Core Operation: Add one spoonful of table salt into the right glass. Use the spoon to stir gently until the salt is evenly mixed.5. Observation Phase: Stop stirring and keep both glasses undisturbed. Continue recording to observe changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both glasses contain uniform, white, opaque milk with no visible clumps.2. After Salt Addition: The right glass gradually shows visible clumping or increased turbidity as small aggregates form; the left glass remains unchanged.3. Comparison Result: A clear difference appears between the two glasses, with aggregation only in the salt-treated milk.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk is a colloidal system containing dispersed protein particles (mainly casein micelles) stabilized by electrostatic repulsion. When salt (NaCl) is added, sodium and chloride ions screen these electrostatic charges, reducing repulsion between protein particles. As a result, the proteins aggregate and form visible clumps, demonstrating ionic interaction screening in colloids.VI. Experimental Notes1. Use identical glasses and equal milk volumes to ensure a fair comparison.2. Keep the camera fixed to clearly capture gradual changes.3. This experiment demonstrates a physical-chemical interaction relevant to biology and food science.

Visibility constraints: both glasses must remain in frame with stable focus to verify causal comparison over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heat Denaturation of Protein Using Egg WhiteI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Heat Denaturation of Protein (Egg White)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of heat on protein structure by observing the denaturation and coagulation of egg white during controlled heating.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tube (1), test tube rack, beaker (water bath), thermometer, hot plate or heat source, fresh egg white (liquid), glass rod or gentle shaking by hand.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a small amount of liquid egg white (about 1/3 volume) into a clean test tube and position it on a test tube rack.2. Water Bath Setup: Pour water into a beaker and place it on a heat source. Insert a thermometer to monitor water temperature.3. Heating Operation: Place the test tube containing egg white into the hot water bath. Heat gradually while gently shaking the test tube to ensure uniform heating.4. Observation: Continue heating and observe changes in the egg white as temperature increases.5. Completion: Remove the test tube once clear changes are observed. Turn off the heat source.IV. Use a water bath instead of direct flame for controlled heating.3. Handle hot equipment carefully to prevent burns.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Latitudinal Radiation Distribution from Equator to PolesSubject: Geography – Physical GeographyObjective: To understand how solar radiation varies with latitude by observing a rotating globe model, recognizing that radiation is highest at the equator and lowest at the poles.II. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDue to Earth’s spherical shape and axial tilt, solar rays strike the equator more directly, concentrating energy over a smaller area and producing high radiation. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Thermostable Catalase and Regular Catalase After Heat TreatmentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermostable Catalase Retains Activity After Heat Exposure2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the enzymatic activity of thermostable catalase and regular catalase after heat exposure by observing oxygen bubble production when hydrogen peroxide is added, and to understand the relationship between enzyme structure, temperature, and catalytic activity.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Clear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 100–150 mL)2. Thermostable catalase solution (red-colored for identification)3. Regular catalase solution (blue-colored for identification)4. Hydrogen peroxide solution (3%, freshly prepared)5. Hot water bath (maintained at 80–90 °C)6. Beaker tongs or heat-resistant gloves7. Dropper or measuring pipette8. Thermometer (optional, for water bath monitoring)9. Camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place two clean, identical clear beakers side by side on the laboratory bench. Add equal volumes (e.g., 20 mL) of red thermostable catalase solution to one beaker and blue regular catalase solution to the other. Ensure both solutions are at room temperature initially.2. Heating Stage: Carefully place both beakers simultaneously into the hot water bath. Heat for the same duration (e.g., 5 minutes), ensuring the liquid levels in the beakers are below the water line of the bath for even heating. Do not stir during heating.3. Removal from Heat: Using tongs or heat-resistant gloves, remove both beakers from the hot water bath and place them back side by side on the bench. Allow them to stand briefly (about 10–20 seconds) to stabilize without cooling significantly.4. Core Reaction Operation: Fix the camera focus and frame so that both beakers are clearly visible throughout the experiment. Using droppers, add an equal volume of hydrogen peroxide (e.g., 5 mL) simultaneously into each beaker.5. Observation and Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording immediately after hydrogen peroxide addition. Observe the formation of bubbles in both beakers without further disturbance.6. Experiment Conclusion: After the reaction subsides, stop recording. Dispose of reaction mixtures according to laboratory safety guidelines and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before adding hydrogen peroxide, both solutions appear colored (red and blue respectively) and show no visible bubbles.2. After Hydrogen Peroxide Addition: The thermostable catalase (red) produces a large number of rapid and continuous oxygen bubbles, often forming visible foam.3. Comparison Result: The regular catalase (blue) produces significantly fewer bubbles or none at all, indicating reduced or lost enzymatic activity after heating.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCatalase catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑). High temperatures can denature enzymes by disrupting their three-dimensional structure, leading to loss of activity. Thermostable catalase possesses a more stable molecular structure that resists heat-induced denaturation, allowing it to retain catalytic activity after heating. Therefore, after heat exposure, thermostable catalase continues to produce oxygen bubbles, while regular catalase shows reduced or no activity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal volumes and concentrations of catalase solutions and hydrogen peroxide are used for fair comparison.2. Handle hot water baths carefully to avoid burns.3. Fix camera position and focus before adding hydrogen peroxide to ensure clear time-lapse comparison.4. Do not touch or move beakers during the reaction to avoid affecting observations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Enzyme thermostability and heat-induced denaturation. Phased storyline: (1) Two identical clear beakers with red thermostable catalase and blue regular catalase are placed side by side; (2) both are heated together in a hot water bath; (3) after heating, hydrogen peroxide is added simultaneously; (4) oxygen bubble formation rapidly appears in the thermostable catalase but is minimal or absent in the regular catalase. Key causal transition: heat exposure leads to differential enzyme activity, verified by unequal bubble production. manual: Urine Phosphate Detection (Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Urine Phosphate Detection by Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric MethodSubject: Healthcare – Renal PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To qualitatively demonstrate the presence of inorganic phosphate in urine by forming a blue-colored molybdenum complex, and to master correct reagent addition order, test tube handling, heating in a water bath, and observation of color change.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsEquipment: Test tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, beaker (water bath), hot plate or alcohol lamp, thermometer (optional), test tube holder.Reagents: Fresh urine sample, acidic ammonium molybdate reagent, reducing agent (such as ascorbic acid or stannous chloride solution), distilled water.Safety: Gloves and goggles; urine treated as a bio-sample.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube in a test tube rack. Using a dropper, add approximately 2 mL of urine sample into the test tube.2. Addition of Molybdate Reagent: Add 1 mL of acidic ammonium molybdate reagent into the test tube. Gently tap or swirl the test tube to mix; do not shake vigorously.3. Addition of Reducing Agent: Add several drops (about 0.5 mL) of the reducing agent to the mixture. Mix gently again.4. Heating: Hold the test tube with a test tube holder and place it into a warm water bath (about 60–70 °C). Heat for 1–2 minutes to accelerate the reaction.5. Reaction and Observation: Remove the test tube from the water bath and place it back on the rack. Allow the reaction to proceed briefly and observe the color change.6. Completion: After observation, dispose of the solution into designated waste, clean glassware, and return equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The urine sample is pale yellow and transparent.After adding ammonium molybdate: The solution remains clear or slightly yellow, with no obvious color change.After adding reducing agent and heating: The solution gradually develops a blue color, ranging from light blue to deep molybdenum blue, indicating the presence of phosphate.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn acidic conditions, inorganic phosphate in urine reacts with ammonium molybdate to form phosphomolybdic acid. Upon addition of a reducing agent and heating, this compound is reduced to molybdenum blue, a blue-colored complex. The intensity of the blue color correlates with the phosphate content, forming the basis of colorimetric phosphate detection used in renal physiology and clinical analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Strictly follow the reagent addition order: urine → ammonium molybdate → reducing agent.2. Mix gently to avoid splashing or contamination.3. Heating should be done in a water bath, not directly over flame.4. Treat urine as potentially infectious material and dispose of waste properly.

manual: Experiment Title: Diffusion Comparison of Liposome-Encapsulated Dye and Free Dye in WaterSubject: Healthcare - PharmacyI. Experiment ObjectiveTo visually compare the diffusion behavior of liposome-encapsulated blue dye versus free blue dye in still water, and to understand how liposomal encapsulation affects molecular diffusion and release.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical clear glass beakers; distilled water; liposome-encapsulated blue dye solution; free blue dye solution of equal apparent color intensity; droppers or pipettes (2); camera with tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass beakers side by side on a stable surface. Add equal volumes of still water to each beaker. Ensure no convection or stirring.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers. Fix focus, exposure, and frame. Start time-lapse recording.3. Dye Addition: Simultaneously add an equal volume of liposome-encapsulated blue dye to the left beaker and free blue dye to the right beaker using separate droppers. Avoid disturbing the water.4. Observation Period: Continue recording as the dyes diffuse naturally. Do not move the beakers.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear diffusion differences are observed.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless water.Early Stage: The free blue dye in the right beaker rapidly disperses downward and outward, forming spreading blue plumes. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFree dye molecules diffuse rapidly in water due to small molecular size and immediate solubility. Experiment Title: Comparison of Iron-Core and Air-Core Electromagnets2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that an electromagnet with an iron core produces a stronger magnetic effect than an air-core electromagnet under the same power conditions, through visual comparison of their ability to lift steel washers.II. Experimental EquipmentInsulated copper wire coils (2 identical coils), soft iron rod (to serve as iron core for one coil), DC power supply or battery (shared power source), switch (single or dual-linked switch), connecting wires, steel washers (multiple identical pieces), non-magnetic tabletop, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse or continuous recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place steel washers flat on the tabletop in two equal piles. Position one coil with an inserted iron core directly above one pile, and the other coil without any core above the second pile, keeping height and orientation the same.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position to capture both coils and washer piles clearly; do not adjust during recording.4. Core Operation: Turn on the power switch. Maintain power for a short, fixed duration suitable for time-lapse demonstration.5. Power Off: Turn off the switch to cut power to both coils simultaneously.6. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Cloud Condensation Nuclei Demonstration with Humid Air and Incense SmokeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Cloud Condensation Nuclei Using Humid Air and Incense Smoke2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) in cloud formation by comparing condensation behavior in humid air with and without aerosol particles, and to understand how cooling leads to cloud droplet formation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical clear transparent chambers with airtight lids2. Humid air source (e.g., warm water vapor or humidifier)3. Incense stick and lighter4. Cooling source (e.g., ice packs, cold plate, or rapid expansion cooling device)5. Camera mounted on a tripod with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography)6. Safety gloves and basic fire safety toolsIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two clear chambers side by side on a stable surface. Ensure both chambers are clean, dry, and identical in volume and shape.2. Humidification: Introduce humid air into both chambers so that the air inside is visibly humid but without condensation on the walls. Seal both chambers.3. Smoke Introduction: Light the incense stick and briefly introduce incense smoke into the left chamber only. Seal the left chamber immediately. Do not add smoke to the right chamber.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera in front of the chambers, ensuring both chambers are fully in frame. Fix the focus and exposure settings. Begin time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Cooling Operation: Apply the cooling source to both chambers simultaneously, ensuring the cooling rate and conditions are as similar as possible.6. In the right chamber, condensation is delayed, weaker, or limited to chamber walls.4. Final State: A clear contrast is observed between the two chambers in droplet density and visibility.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCooling humid air reduces its capacity to hold water vapor. When the air becomes supersaturated, excess water vapor condenses into liquid droplets. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mercury Detection Using Thioacetamide Test Strip MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mercury Detection in Food by Thioacetamide Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of mercury in a food sample by preparing a food extract, reacting it with a thioacetamide-based mercury test strip, observing color change, and understanding the detection principle.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBeaker (100–250 mL), prepared food extract solution (clear filtrate), thioacetamide-based mercury test strips, original unused strip (control), tweezers or gloved hands, stopwatch or timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the beaker on a stable surface. Pour an appropriate volume of prepared food extract solution into the beaker, ensuring the liquid is clear and sufficient to immerse the test strip reaction zone.2. Initial Comparison: Place one unused mercury test strip beside the beaker as the original reference strip.3. Core Operation: Using tweezers or gloved fingers, hold a mercury test strip and immerse its reactive end vertically into the food extract solution. Ensure full contact between the strip’s reaction zone and the solution.4. Reaction: Keep the strip in the solution for a short, fixed time (several seconds). For demonstration, the reaction process may be accelerated using time-lapse photography.5. Removal and Comparison: Remove the strip from the solution and place it flat beside the original unused strip for direct visual comparison.6. Completion: Observe and record the color change, then properly dispose of used strips according to safety requirements.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThioacetamide in the test strip hydrolyzes under test conditions to release sulfide ions. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Colorimetric LAMP Reaction Showing Solution Color ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Colorimetric LAMP Reaction Showing Solution Color Change2. Subject: Healthcare - Medicine - Molecular Diagnostics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) can detect target DNA through a visible color change, and to compare results between a sample containing target DNA and a negative control.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials- Two identical clear reaction tubes- Colorimetric LAMP reaction mix (with pH-sensitive indicator)- DNA sample containing target sequence- Negative control (nuclease-free water or buffer)- Micropipette and tips- Tube rack- Heated block or water bath set to 60–65 °C- Camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear tubes on a rack on the lab bench. Ensure the camera is fixed and focused on both tubes for continuous observation.2. Reagent Addition: Add equal volumes of colorimetric LAMP mix into each tube.3. Sample Loading: Add the DNA sample to one tube (labelled sample) and add an equal volume of negative control to the other tube (labelled control).4. Mixing: Gently tap or briefly spin the tubes to mix contents without creating bubbles.5. Incubation: Place both tubes together into the heated block set at 60–65 °C.6. Time-lapse Observation: Incubate for the designated reaction time while recording. Do not disturb the tubes during incubation.7. Completion: Remove tubes and place them back on the bench for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes appear the same color, typically pink or red, indicating no amplification.2. During Incubation: The sample tube gradually changes color as amplification proceeds, while the control tube remains unchanged.3. Final Result: The sample tube shows a clear color shift (e.g., pink to yellow), indicating presence of target DNA; the control tube retains the original color.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesColorimetric LAMP is an isothermal DNA amplification technique. Experiment Title: Surface Ripples Generated by a Submerged Vibration Source2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science (Wave Phenomena)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how continuous vibrations generated beneath the water surface propagate through water and form visible surface ripples; to recognize water waves as energy transfer through a medium rather than mass transfer; to learn basic methods of observing wave patterns using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentClear rectangular water tank (1), clean water (filled to about 3/4 of tank height), small vibration source or waterproof vibrator (1), power supply or switch for vibration source, support or suction mount to fix the vibration source, camera or smartphone with tripod, lighting source (optional, for clear observation), ruler or marker (optional, for reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the clear water tank on a stable horizontal surface. Fill it with clean water until the water surface is calm and free of bubbles. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at a slight angle to the water surface so the entire surface is visible. Fix the focus and exposure settings to prevent automatic changes. Set the camera to time-lapse or continuous recording mode.4. Core Operation: Switch on the vibration source to produce continuous, steady vibrations. Do not move the tank or the vibration source during operation.5. Observation and Recording: Allow the vibration to continue for several seconds while recording. Adjust time base to show several carrier cycles and adjust voltage scale to clearly view the waveform envelope.4. Power On: Turn on the power supply and activate the AM transmitter. Verify that a steady carrier waveform appears on the oscilloscope when no sound is applied.5. Core Operation: Speak softly into the microphone and observe the waveform on the oscilloscope. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAmplitude Modulation (AM) is a process in which the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier signal is varied in proportion to a lower-frequency information signal. In this experiment, the microphone converts sound pressure into an electrical audio signal. This audio signal controls the amplitude of the carrier generated by the transmitter. On the oscilloscope, the carrier frequency stays constant, while the envelope shape and height represent the instantaneous amplitude of the audio signal. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Warm Dyed Water Rising in a Convection Tank (Buoyant Parcel Demonstration)2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate and visualize the concept of a buoyant air parcel in the atmosphere by observing warm, red-dyed water rising in a still convection tank; to understand how temperature differences create density differences that drive buoyant motion.II. Experimental EquipmentConvection tank (transparent rectangular tank filled with clear, still water), water heater or hot water source, thermometer (optional), red food dye, syringe or dropper (for injection), small container for warm dyed water, ruler or scale attached to tank wall (optional for height reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Fill the convection tank with clear water and allow it to stand until the water is completely still. Ensure no visible currents remain.2. Dye Preparation: Prepare a small volume of warm water (noticeably warmer than the tank water but not boiling). Add red dye and mix until the color is uniform.3. Injection Setup: Draw the warm red-dyed water into a syringe or dropper. Position the syringe tip gently at the bottom center of the tank, avoiding disturbance to the surrounding water.4. Core Operation: Slowly inject a small blob of the warm red-dyed water at the bottom of the tank, then stop applying pressure and release it completely.5. Observation: Observe the motion of the dyed water blob as it detaches and moves upward through the clear water.6. Completion: Continue observing until the dyed water slows, spreads, or mixes with the surrounding water. Do not stir the tank during observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The tank water is clear and motionless; the dyed water is concentrated near the bottom at the injection point.2. Rising Stage: After release, the red-dyed water forms a coherent blob or plume that rises vertically upward from the bottom.3. Development Stage: As it rises, the blob may expand, form a mushroom-like shape, and gradually lose its sharp boundary due to mixing.4. Final Stage: The dyed water slows, spreads laterally, and eventually mixes with the surrounding water, becoming less distinct.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Buoyancy caused by density differences.2. Principle Analysis: Warm water has a lower density than the surrounding cooler water. When released at the bottom of the tank, the warm dyed water experiences an upward buoyant force. This force causes it to rise, analogous to a warm air parcel ascending in the atmosphere.3. Atmospheric Analogy: In atmospheric science, warm air parcels rise through cooler surrounding air due to buoyancy, leading to convection, cloud formation, and vertical transport of heat and moisture.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the tank water is still before injection to avoid interference from background currents.2. Inject the dyed water slowly to prevent artificial turbulence.3. Use only a small temperature difference to maintain safe handling and clear visualization.4. Avoid shaking or moving the tank during observation.

manual: Title: Visualization Experiment of the Vertex of an Upward-Opening Quadratic FunctionI. Basic InformationSubject: Mathematics – Quadratic FunctionsObjective: To visually understand the vertex and axis of symmetry of an upward-opening quadratic function through graphical representation.II. Experimental SetupBackground: White backgroundCoordinate System: Cartesian coordinate system with x∈[-4,4], y∈[-1,8]Graph Elements: Purple solid curve for the quadratic function, red point for the vertex, blue dashed line for the axis of symmetry.III. Experimental Procedure1. Draw a Cartesian coordinate system on a white background, labeling x- and y-axes with the specified ranges.2. Plot the quadratic function y = x² − 2x + 1 using a purple solid line, ensuring the parabola opens upward.3. Identify the vertex by calculation or observation and mark it with a red dot at (1,1), labeling the coordinates.4. Draw a blue dashed vertical line representing the axis of symmetry at x = 1.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. The plotted parabola opens upward and is symmetric about the vertical line x = 1.2. The lowest point of the parabola is clearly visible at the red-marked vertex (1,1).3. Points on the parabola are mirrored on both sides of the axis of symmetry.V. Experimental Principle SummaryFor a quadratic function y = ax² + bx + c with a > 0, the graph is an upward-opening parabola. The vertex occurs at x = −b/(2a). For y = x² − 2x + 1, a = 1 and b = −2, giving x = 1. Substituting x = 1 yields y = 1, so the vertex is (1,1). The line x = 1 is the axis of symmetry, dividing the parabola into two mirror-image halves.

Demonstration Materials and ConditionsFlowering plants of the same species (with visible stamens and pistils), honeybee (real observation in nature or simulated/animated demonstration), outdoor garden or greenhouse environment with sufficient light, close-up observation tools (camera or magnifier, optional).III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate from Ammonia and Hydrogen ChlorideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate by Gas Diffusion2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when ammonia vapor and hydrogen chloride vapor diffuse and meet in air, they react to form fine ammonium chloride particulate, simulating secondary aerosol formation in the atmosphere.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass chamber with two opposite openings or inlets; ammonia source (concentrated ammonia solution with cotton or ammonia gas generator); hydrogen chloride source (concentrated hydrochloric acid with cotton or HCl gas generator); tweezers; rubber stoppers or lids; camera with fixed focus and tripod; protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass chamber on a stable surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the chamber and lock focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.2. Gas Placement: Using tweezers, place an ammonia-soaked cotton at one side inlet of the chamber and a hydrogen chloride–soaked cotton at the opposite side inlet.3. Release and Recording: Simultaneously open or unseal both sides to allow ammonia vapor and hydrogen chloride vapor to diffuse into the chamber. Start time-lapse recording without moving the camera.4. Observation Period: Allow the gases to diffuse and mix naturally in the chamber for a short period until visible particulate appears.5. Completion: Seal the chamber, stop recording, and ventilate the area safely after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chamber is clear and transparent with no visible particles.2. During Diffusion: Invisible gases spread from opposite sides toward the center of the chamber.3. Mixing Zone: A white, smoke-like particulate gradually appears where the two gases meet.4. Final State: The white particulate becomes denser at the interface region, forming a visible band or cloud of ammonium chloride.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAmmonia (NH3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) are gaseous substances that diffuse through air. When they meet, they undergo an acid–base reaction forming solid ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) as fine particulate matter. This process models the formation of secondary inorganic aerosols in the atmosphere.Core Reaction: NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s)VI. Experimental Precautions1. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area or fume hood.2. Avoid direct inhalation of gases; wear goggles and gloves.3. Ensure the camera remains fixed to maintain consistent observation.4. Dispose of chemical materials according to safety regulations.
